In the *Pañcastavī*, the second hymn, the *Carcastava*,
is for the most part a path that rests upon the abode of the Śākta power, which prescribes manifold injunctions.
For men, it is that certain creeper which, when ascended through the power of meditation, bestows a multitude of various fruits;
nor is it in the soulless and fruitless abode of the individual self (puṃdhāman), nor in the Supreme,
but rather it is some indescribable creeper that flashes forth with vast fruit for the attainment of one's desired goal.
Now, desiring to commence the second *Carcastava*, the Master—
wishing for its completion without obstacles— contemplates the lotus-feet of the Mother as being embraced by the nectar of the heroic-erotic (*vīra-śṛṅgāra*) rasa.
Oṃ, salutations to Tripurasundarī—
[upon whose head] the garland released by Purandara, beautiful with bliss, was forcibly placed by Mahiṣāsura [as he lay prostrate].
May the lotus-foot of Ambikā, enchanting with the tinkling of her beautiful anklets, lead to my victory. || 1 ||

Ambikā is the supreme power (*parā-vāk*), who is skillful in beholding the manifestation of the self as the fullness of the state of "I" (*ahambhāva*), and who possesses excellence beyond all else. As it is said in the *Catuḥśatikā*:
"When she perceives the manifestation of the Self, she is that supreme digit (*kalā*)."
Having assumed the form of Ambikā, the Supreme Speech was uttered.
Thus [it is said]. Also in the *Śrīpratyabhijñā*:
"Consciousness, whose nature is reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*), is the supreme speech (*parā vāk*) arising from its own inherent savor (1.5.13)."

Thus, may the lotus-foot—the foot itself being a lotus due to its possession of qualities such as softness and fragrance—of that Ambikā, the Śakti who is the mother of the universe, be for my victory; that is, for me to attain *vijaya*, the acquisition of a station superior to the entire world. This is expressed through the optative suffix (*lot*) in the sense of a prayer (*āśaṃsā*). "For victory" (*vijayāya*).

The status of being a recipient (*sampradānatva*) is established by the rule *tumarthācca bhāvavacanāt*. Furthermore, "victory" (*vijaya*) means the state of being the controller of all, for the purpose of attaining that; for this is how it was explained by the Teachers in the *Kauṣītaky-upaniṣad* passage: "Whatever victory belongs to a Brāhmaṇa, whatever prosperity... and so forth. The same applies in what follows.
In the utterance of the word "victory" (*jaya*), the meaning should be understood according to its contextual application. Here,
since it is generally the right foot that is renowned for its skillful dexterity (*dākṣiṇya*) due to its utility in delivering the intended kick, it should be understood as the "right lotus-foot."

Alternatively, in battle, due to the intensity of one's engagement and the necessity of striking suddenly when the opportunity for a blow arises, either the left or the right foot may be used without distinction. Or else, the crushing of the demon Mahiṣāsura is the work of a single foot alone; thus, his heroic prowess is manifested.
With this intention, the singular number is employed. Of what sort was it upon the crest—meaning the crown—of the demon Mahiṣāsura?

Or rather, it refers to his head as characterized by that crest; [it was] placed there with force—that is, by a rash act—such that he struck a blow by which the Asura reached the end of his life in battle. Therefore...
"Her glorious lotus-feet are adorned with tinkling jeweled anklets"—
according to this statement from the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*, since it is fitting that the sound of tinkling should arise from her lotus-feet at that time,
[she is] charming with the sweet and delightful jingling of her anklets (*mañjīra*), that is, the *jhaṇat*-sounds of her foot-ornaments.
It captivates the hearts of his own devotees and shatters the hearts of his adversaries; likewise,
it is beautiful with the joy and delight born from the destruction of invincible enemies,
or it is desirable due to the rapture that indicates the good fortune of attaining the future state of supreme lordship.

It is that [place] in which garlands— consisting of clusters of divine, wonderful, fragrant, and variegated flowers— were released and cast down by Purandara, the Lord of Devas, on the occasion of worshipping the lotus-feet of the Bhagavatī at a time appropriate for victory;
or else, it is where Ānanda, Śrīputra, Sundara, Kāmeśvara, Purandara, Indra, or Tripurāri [performed such acts].
"By them released garland" (*tairmuktamālya*) means a flower-garland being bound [to the deity] at the time of worship.
This is what is intended: that the Blessed Lady’s foot-strike, accompanied by its tinkling sound, was such that it then [acted as] for Indra.

In the same way, that very lotus-foot— which was the cause of victory— is now being recollected in the mind, manifested through the aesthetic emotions (bhāvas) such as joy associated with it, and experienced through excitants (uddīpanas) such as the tinkling of anklets.
He expresses the hope: "May this [work], as it comes to be relished within the heart, lead even me to the exuberance of a supreme excellence of the wonder of intense, supramundane bliss.
Here, there is a *saṃkara* (commixture) of the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and heroic (*vīra*) sentiments, because they appear clearly due to their sharing a single substratum.

The secret of the tradition of the *caraṇavidyā* is not disclosed, because it must be strictly guarded and because it is to be understood from the mouth of the Guru alone. Were it revealed, the intention behind its description as a singular entity would be understood;
nor would there be any contradiction with the established renown of its designation as a "pair" (*yugala*). || 1 ||
Now, he indicates the fruits corresponding to the propriety of worshipping even those manifestations of Śrī Devī that are partial aspects of her vidyā:
"O Tripurā! Victorious are you, the source of beauty and grace, the wish-fulfilling trees for the attainment of sovereignty over the worlds!"
O Mother of the World! May these prostrations before you be like full moons that awaken the clusters of night-lotuses of poetic talent. || 2 ||
O Mother of the World! O Tripurā! She is Tripurā because she possesses three cities (*purāṇi*) consisting of the body, the intellect, and the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Thus, the Śrīcakra is of the nature of these three cities: the first city consists of the square, the sixteen-petaled lotus, and the eight-petaled lotus;
the second consists of the fourteen-spoked and the twelve-spoked wheels; and [the third] consists of the eight-spoked wheel, the triangle, and the Bindu-cakra.

It is determined in the secret scriptures that "the third city" refers to this. As for the other [cities], they have been mentioned previously and will also be described later in their proper places. O You, these prostrations—these salutations offered by us who are bowed low with devotion toward You—are victorious.

There exist those who possess the quality of bestowing the fruit of supreme excellence. Of what sort? They are the earths—the sources and places of origin—for beauty, fortune, amorous graces, and the playful manifestations of the mind’s instability born of passion (*śṛṅgāra*). As it has been said:
"The instability of mental fluctuations arising from the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) is considered to be *vibhrama* (bewilderment).
Here, because the plural number is contained within the compound, by means of the word "etc. (*ādi*) which is thereby obtained, *vilāsa*, *līlā*, and so forth [are included].

The *hāvas*, *bhāvas*, and so forth are also to be understood as objects of apprehension. Among these, *vibhrama* (bewilderment) is a state of confusion produced by intoxication, passion, or joy. For example: rising from one's seat without cause and departing elsewhere; interrupting a conversation initiated by a lover and engaging in talk with a female friend; feigning anger and indignation for no reason; and the sudden begging for flowers and other such things.

Its abandonment consists in the tearing and discarding of garments, ornaments, and garlands without cause, as well as their mental disregard. Some, however, say that *vibhrama* is the transformation arising from the youth of women. As it has been said:
"It is the intoxication of youth alone that teaches the graceful charms (*lalita*) of amorous women."
Thus, in all these cases, the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgārarasa*) alone is the cause. Furthermore, of what nature are they?

They are like wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpataru*) for the attainment—that is, the abundance—of sovereignty, the universal empire over the worlds; likewise, they are [the causes] of poetic compositions, the works of poets.

Regarding the clusters— that is, the multitudes— of *kumuda* and *kuvalaya* flowers, which are of the nature of poems characterized by the eighteen marks, differentiated by the categories of the visible (such as drama) and the audible (poetry), and composed of sentiments such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*); [this refers to] the expansion of knowledge, that is, the blossoming of understanding, concerning them.

"Full moons" refers to those like the full moon of the Rākā night, which bring about the play of speech; by these three qualifiers, it is indicated that through the worship of the Great Mantra of Mahātripurasundarī, which consists of three syllables (kūṭas),
one attains the threefold fruit— among which, regarding the worship of the first syllable:
It should be understood that through the grace of Sarasvatī, the power of poetic composition (*kavitva-śakti*) is generated by the worship of the second *kūṭa*;
through the grace of Kāmarāja, its presiding deity, beauty and other qualities are generated by the worship of the third;
and through His grace, the attainment of sovereignty is achieved. As for the fruits of the means of accomplishing the *Śakti-kūṭa* and so forth:
In the Vāmakeśvara [Tantra]:
"O Great Goddess! I shall proclaim the means of accomplishment for the Peak-syllable of Power (Śaktikūṭa).
Having created [the universe] in the form of the seed-syllable of Power, she then withdraws it."
One should contemplate [the process] within the body from the beginning of creation until its dissolution;
then, O Goddess of Gods, one becomes like another Vainateya.
O Goddess! From the sight of the Nāgas, this [mantra] causes the paralysis of embodied beings;
it is like a steady rain-cloud pouring down a shower of nectar.
It destroys chronic and artificial poisons, as well as natural and synthetic toxins;
it overcomes malignant diseases, planetary influences, and the hosts of *anoka*, *dākinīs*, and *rūpikās*.
He appears like the Three-Eyed One [Śiva] to the hosts of *bhūtas*, *pretas*, and *piśācas*;
or rather, by him this Vidyā is contemplated as being perfectly complete.
O Great Goddess! situated in the center of the birth-mandala, the heart-lotus, and the face-mandala, she alone possesses a radiance equal to that of a ruby.
The eightfold sovereignty over her arises for him without delay,
even if the practitioner merely remembers her name in his mind.
At that very moment, O beloved, he becomes known to the circle of Mothers,
as soon as he recites the mantra of Mahātripurasundarī.
At that very moment, the command of the Mother-circle (mātṛcakra) descends into his body;
he shall become beloved by all the yoginīs who abide in every station.
O Supreme Goddess! Indeed, by meditation alone, the practitioner [attains this] as if toward a son;
but when, O Supreme Goddess, he worships the Fully Perfected One (Paripūrṇā), [he attains liberation].
At that very moment, they bestow upon him the supreme siddhi of Khecarī;
for there are sixty-four crores of highly powerful Yoginīs who are self-restrained.
O Goddess worshipped by heroes! Having taken recourse to this wheel, [the deities] are established:
first in the related positions, then the eight seed-syllables in the middle, and finally on the outside.
Having meditated upon the *kalā* on the stage, the woman becomes as dear as the bodiless god of love (*Anaṅga*).
O Supreme Goddess, for each one of the vidyās beginning with Karaśuddhi, [this is the procedure].
In the Rudrayāmala Tantra, however, the ritual action was previously described by me:
having become Madana through intoxicants, [one acts] with nooses, goads, bows, and arrows.

O Goddess of the gods! in that same way, one whose body has been made into the three cities (tripurīkṛta) by means of the Śaktis agitates the women of the heavens, the earth, and the depths of the netherworld.
One may accomplish even the Siddhas, Gandharvas, Devas, and Vidyādharas;
therein, in the Great Vajra Array, the Śaktis are produced as arrows.
The *mādana* syllables are placed after the first [syllable] and at the very end;
the *mahāpāśa*, which resides at the beginning and the end, is proclaimed to be of human origin (*pauruṣeya*).
The power of Rudra, known as Kuṇḍalinī, is Māyā; she is called the feminine bond (strīpāśa).
O Pārvatī, in the group of vowels, the fourth is Aruṇā, and the second is also [Māyā].
"The pair of male and female bows, and the goad that pervades the fire of desire. Thus [ends verse] 2.
Now, casting aside the conceit of being the author of praise within his own self, he manifests shame regarding his own composition among the worshippers:
"O Goddess! Even those such as Vācaspati, whose minds are intent upon the task of praise, become stupefied."
Therefore, O Consort of the burner of Tripura, what am I but one born of innate dullness to compose a hymn to You here? || 3 ||

O wife of the burner of Tripura! [The term] *Tripura* refers to a Daitya; *Tāpana* is the burner or destroyer of him, namely Śiva; his wife is she whose body is never separated from him—this is the address: "O Queen of the Supreme Brahman! O Goddess!
O you who are intent on the play of creating the universe, beginning with Śiva and ending with the earth! In the midst of your hymn of praise...

Even the learned ones such as Vācaspati and others— Bṛhaspati and his peers— whose intellects are as sharp as the tip of a blade of kuśa grass and whose minds are intent on the task of praising and describing your qualities, become stupefied; though they are not dull-witted, they become as if inert and fall silent, for "words turn back from you along with the mind, unable to reach you."

According to the Śruti: "O Śāṇḍilya, [He is]... (Śāṇḍilya Upani�sad 2.3). This means that even among those [the Vedas], there is no manifestation of speech—which is Your very form—without Your will. In that case, what need is there to mention those of dull intellect like myself?
By the word "api" (even), it is implied that even the Vedas are incapable [of describing You]. For they [the Vedas] proceed by way of injunction (*vidhi*).

And being intent on providing instruction, they point [to the goal] with modesty by means of an indirect definition (*taṭasthalakṣaṇa*), according to the maxim of the "coarse Arundhatī" (*sthūlārundhatīnyāya*). As it was said by the venerable teacher Bhāskararāya in his *Śivastava*:
"O Supreme Śiva, even the Vedas, which are all-knowing and dear to you as your very life-breath, [point to you] by way of direct identification (*śṛṅgagrāhikayā*)."
As if possessed by modesty, they do not speak directly to you;
yet they repeatedly deny others with their words, saying "not this, not that. If even there, who else but a person like me would repeat to you, "It is thus"?
Thus [it is said]. The author of the work himself also states in the fifth hymn:
"The heads of the Vedas, though naturally hard, have become exceedingly tender...
"How can they find Your footprints in the tender sprouts, O Pārvatī? (Śloka 24).

For this reason, while the present context concerns the calculation of the intellectual capacities of Vācaspati and others, Your hymn is merely a recitation of worldly qualities (*laukikaguṇānuvāda*), and that is of six kinds. As it has been said:
Salutation, benediction, statement of the established doctrine, valor, majesty,
and prayer— these are the six characteristics of a hymn of praise.

Thus: among those such as Vācaspati and others, who am I—not even one worthy of being counted—that could be identified as "this one" or "that one," capable of composing a Vedic *stotra* which consists in the description of qualities residing in a subject (*guṇin*) accomplished by means of chanted mantras (*pragīta-mantra-sādhya*)? For I am, by my very nature, inherently dull-witted (*nisarga-jaḍima*).

The meaning is: "I, being of dull intellect, feel great shame because of my restlessness in desiring to exert myself toward a reality that even those such as Vācaspati cannot engage with. As it is said in the *Śrī-lalitā-stava-ratna*:
"Who indeed on earth is more capable than I to praise the Reality who dwells in the lap of Śiva?"
Let it be so; by virtue of my long-accumulated merits, may that [which I desire] be manifested before me.
Thus [ends the third section].

Anticipating the objection, "In that case, since composing a hymn of praise is impossible, why do you exert yourself with the desire to do so?", he reveals his own helplessness in the face of the sentiment of devotion (bhakti-rasa):
"O Mother, nevertheless, for the sake of quenching the intense heat of worldly existence, I am the helmsman of the great ocean of Your praise."
[An alternative reading is *stavamahārṇava*.
O Bhavānī! That grasp of devotion to your lotus-feet compels me, somehow, to speak in praise.
O Mother, O Universal Progenitor, O Bhavānī, O Consort of Bhava! Nevertheless, even though Bhava is by nature insentient, [in you...]

In order to bring about the cessation— the cutting off— of the intense and unbearable torments of saṃsāra, namely the threefold internal and other afflictions, he [seeks] to praise you, who are personally realized.
Regarding Your lotus feet— Your two lotus feet— it is devotion characterized by an exceedingly intense affection; it is a "graha" (seizing possession),
an immersion consisting of being rendered helpless by the absorption in the nectar-essence of Your lotus feet— an experience that is truly beyond all calculation.

It makes me talkative; it forcibly compels me to offer praise. Of what nature is this praise? It is like a great ocean—a vast sea that is difficult to fathom due to its boundless profundity and other qualities—and [this praise] is the helmsman therein.

Because it carries one to the further shore, it is a "boatman" (potavāhaka). Just as by means of a boatman one is led to the other side of the ocean, so too may devotion to you alone lead even a dull-witted person like me to the further shore of praise—this is the intended meaning. Furthermore, even this deficiency of speech would cease as soon as your glance falls upon me.
Because of the cessation of the flow of the stream [of worldly existence]. As it was said by Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇa:
"O Śambhu! If you do not will it, who is able to bend even a blade of grass?
But who, favored by your will, would not bear the burden of Brahmā? (Stava-cintāmaṇi 93). || 4 ||

Now, one might object: "Are not Viṣṇu, Viriñci, and the others alone worthy of praise, since they are the agents of the creation and so forth of the universe, and not I? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"O Bhavānī, you give birth to the worlds; you sustain them; and you remain awake for their destruction."
You shatter delusion, yet you obstruct it; you prevail over playful dalliance—this of yours is a marvel! || 5 ||

O Bhavānī! You give birth to, that is, you create, the worlds consisting of the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*) beginning with Śiva and ending with Earth (*kṣiti*). For the *Śruti* states: "That from which these beings are born, by which, once born, they live, and into which they enter when they depart—that is Brahman" (*Taittirīya Upaniṣad* 3.1). Therefore, from this very Self (*ātman*), space (*ākāśa*) [is produced].

From space arises air, from air fire, from fire water, and from water earth— thus according to the scriptural account of creation ending with the earth (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1). Just as from a well-kindled fire thousands of sparks of similar form emanate, so it is here.
For it is stated in the Śruti: "In this same way, various gentle states are born from the Imperishable, and into it they also go" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.1), and also:
"Just as tiny sparks fly forth from a fire" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.20).
The Yājñavalkya Smṛti also says:
Just as sparks fly forth from a heated mass of iron,
even so do individual selves indeed emerge from the Self.

Thus [it is said]. However, the object of creation exists internally through identity (*tādātmya*), for otherwise a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of that object would be impossible. As it has been stated:
"The Lord [possesses] the latent impression (*vāsana*) of the entire multitude of entities residing within Himself."
"Indeed, it exists; for without it, the impulse of desire does not proceed" (Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā 1.5.10).

This is because of the Śruti: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1), and "Brahman is one only, without a second" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1). Also, in the Paiṅgalopaniṣad (1.1): "In the beginning..."
It will be stated:
"Everything from Śiva down to the earth resides within Your belly, O You whose body consists of the three coils" (Somaśambhu-jaya-stava 29).
Thus, by mere will—according to the Vedic revelation, "May I become many; therefore, He made Himself manifold"—[the universe is created].
Because the universe is produced through a gradual progression [of stages], Consciousness—
by its own will, unfolding the universe within its own screen (Pratyabhijñāhṛdayasūtra 2)— is autonomous and the cause of the manifestation of the universe (Pratyabhijñāhṛdayasūtra 1).
By its own will alone, it swallows and also emits the entire universe; thus,

having painted the variegated universe within itself with the brush of its own will— according to the system of the Śaiva Āgamas, there are two hundred and twenty-four worlds, though according to other systems [the number differs].

She gives birth to— that is, she creates— the fourteen worlds characterized as Bhūr, Bhuvas, and Svar, which constitute the path of the universe; for Brahman, when not permeated by Bhavānī in the form of Brahmī-śakti,
is incapable of the act of creating the world, being devoid of power.

Because they are largely inert like stone and the like, and because they lack movement and thus depend on others, their state of dependence is very clear; therefore, the meaning is that in reality, the creation of the world and so forth truly occurs, as she—whose nature consists of those various powers—effects them. She truly brings them into being, maintains them, sustains them, and nourishes them.

By implication, she becomes the Vaiṣṇavī power and performs that task; for, as before, even Viṣṇu lacks the capacity to accomplish his own work without being permeated by that power. Here, by the repeated use of the word "becomes" (*bhavati*), the sense of restriction is to be understood: she *indeed* becomes [the power], and no other.
This is the meaning. The same should be understood for what follows as well. Likewise, regarding those worlds that have been created, sustained, and nourished:

For the sake of destruction, she indeed remains awake—she is vigilant—in order to withdraw [the universe] at the proper time and according to its own nature, abiding within herself as the essence of the seed (*bījātman*), but not to bring about total annihilation; nor does she ever resort there to a state of negligence. In this case as well, as before, she is in the form of the power Raudrī.
It should be understood that having manifested and withdrawn [the universe], it performs the work of the presiding Lord Rudra.
Thus, there arises indeed the Āṇava-mala, which consists of delusion (moha) and the sense of being incomplete;

from this arise the fifty cognitive states (pratyayas), such as the misconceptions beginning with darkness (tamas) and delusion (moha), and those known as the powers (śakti), contentments (tuṣṭi), and accomplishments (siddhi).
This is observed as it was stated in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"Tamas, moha, mahāmoha, tāmisra, and that which is called andhatāmisra—
this fivefold ignorance has manifested from the Great Self."

Thus, the power named Jyeṣṭhā, having manifested by expanding her own multitude of rays, rescues those souls submerged in the ocean of delusion who have been pierced by the descent of the supreme power (*paraśaktipāta*),
and fashions the effect which is the fifth causal principle known as Sadāśiva; in that very manner, she obstructs [the lower states].
Because it is untouched by the power of another (paraśakti), it conceals living beings blinded by māyā; that is, it effects the obscuration of their own true nature (svarūpa).

Here, in the causal state called Īśvara, this is accomplished through the power called Aiśvarya, as previously described. By this, the fourth function (kṛtya) should be understood to have been stated.
As it is said in the Bhāgavata:
"Śakti creates the universe; she indeed protects everything;
by her will, she destroys this world of moving and non-moving beings."
Neither Viṣṇu, nor Hara, nor Indra, nor Brahmā, nor Pāvaka, nor Arka,
nor Varuṇa are able to accomplish their respective tasks in any way whatsoever.
For joined with her, those gods perform their respective duties;
she is perceived directly as the cause in all undertakings.
By this it is stated that the agency of creation and so forth is established through direct perception and other means of valid cognition as belonging to Śakti alone. As it is said elsewhere:
"Even Śiva becomes a corpse when he is devoid of Kuṇḍalinī."
Even one who is devoid of power is considered by the wise to be incapable.
Thus, this fivefold activity— wondrous, marvelous,
and diverse— is Your playful sport (*līlāyita*); *līlā* is an activity performed for no other purpose.

Alternatively, it means that the playful movement (*khelāyitam*)—which is the obscuration of that [state]—is performed effortlessly, being caused by an excess of one's own joy. As it was said by Bhāskararāya in his *Devīstava*:
"Even Śiva is not the master over the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the gods headed by Brahmā and Viṣṇu."
O Mother of the World! This is Your manner: for a moment, the plucking of *uddālaka* flowers.

*Uddālaka* is the name of a particular game. "It triumphs" means it prevails with excellence due to the abundance of the essence of joy (*āhlāda-rasa*). The sense is that, according to the previously stated principle—that it unfolds the universe within its own wall by its own will—this [state] surges forth as a dense mass from the flow of the essence of intense bliss (*nirbhara-ānanda-rasa*). This is the underlying intention here.

The supreme power consisting of Agni and Soma, even while engaged in the play (*līlā*) whose nature is the concealment of her own form, practices the fivefold task (*kṛtyapañcaka*) characterized by self-recognition (*pratyabhijñā*); through that, she should manifest her own Self, which is a mass of consciousness and bliss, as the ninth [state]. Thus it has been said:
"Salutation to Śiva, who eternally performs the fivefold acts, who illumines the ultimate reality of one's own self as a mass of consciousness and bliss" (Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya, verse 9).
Thus it is stated in the *Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya*; nevertheless, "in that same way, He performs the fivefold acts" (Sūtra 10).

And their characteristics are defined right there [in that same work] as being established through appearance (*ābhāsana*), coloring (*rañjana*), reflective awareness (*vimarśana*), and the state of the seed (*bījāvasthāpana*) (Sūtra 11).
Thus, by means of this turn of phrase—suggesting that even those who have merely become vessels for the grace of the Blessed Goddess desire it—he expresses the wondrous nature of her majesty, saying:
"O Gaurī, as fair as the petal of a fresh lotus! Even upon one in whom [your grace] has appeared only slightly... [the grace which is sweet with favor...]
You cast your gaze;
upon it, the continuous streams of glances from women, scattered by the arrows of the bodiless god of love, fall without interruption.
O you who are as fair as the petals of a fresh lotus! [That] *ambuja* is a lotus which is *nava*, meaning new, freshly blossomed, or just now opened.
Those leaves which are of a glossy, reddish hue—addressing her whose complexion is likewise fair (gaura), one uses this appropriate invocation: "O Gaurī! O Kātyāyanī! As it is said in the Devīpurāṇa:
"She who was consumed by the fire of yoga and was born again from the Himalayas..."
And because her color is like that of a conch, a kunda flower, or the moon, she is therefore remembered as Gaurī.
Thus, this is either Gaurī, the presiding deity of the Kānyakubja seat; as it is said in the Pādma Purāṇa:
"Likewise, Gaurī is in Kānyakubja.
Alternatively, when, by the command of Brahmā, the Goddess manifested herself in the form of white and black colors.

At that time, she became renowned by names such as Gaurī and others. As it is stated in the Vāyu Purāṇa: "There, she who was the illustrious one forming half the body of Śaṅkara—her right half of the body was white, and likewise her left was fair."
"Divide yourself," was the command given to the Goddess by Svayambhū;
at that very moment, O twice-born ones, she became twofold as Gaurī and Kālī.
Thus: toward that servant who is to be favored, you have cast—even if but slightly—your gaze, which is sweet, meaning endowed with sweetness and charming to the heart;
a side-glance moist with the essence of compassion, while remaining in his presence.

The usage here is as if it were present. In that assembly of people who became the targets for the side-long glances [of the women], there were certain women—lovers afflicted by the fever of passion—who were pierced and struck by the five arrows of Anaṅga (Smara), consisting of flowers such as the Aśoka; the continuous streams of the eyes, the rows of their glances, [fell upon him].

The meaning is that they cast their passionate glances toward him incessantly and without ceasing for the sake of quelling the fever of love. Here, although you alone are present as the cause for the act of casting glances, the glances of the others also fall [upon him] according to the maxim of the pigeons on a threshing floor.

By the phrase "may they be," there is the figure of speech *samuccaya* (accumulation) due to the interruption of the narrative flow. Here, by the word *anaṅga* ("bodiless"), it is indicated that Smara has no rival whatsoever because he lacks a physical body. For this very reason, since those women have no other means [of relief], [the poet intends] for the pacification of their suffering.

It should be understood that because one has not yet obtained the vision of the Mother’s grace—which directly dispels suffering—one must long for those people who have been so favored by Her. Furthermore, the fruit of the practice of the second seed-syllable is likewise the subjugation of all. (6)
Now, encouraging the devotee by way of the example of the renowned Emperor, he declares the majesty of the dust of the lotus-feet:
"Even for that preeminent Udayana, the lord of the earth, whose footstool was kissed by the prostrations of the Vidyādharas..."
This very attainment of the status of a universal monarch is a grace born from a single atom of dust from the lotus-feet of Your Honor.

The word "he" (iti) should be supplied, and its meaning as a vocative is to be understood as before. Now, "gā" refers to the Goddess whose nature is illumination and so forth, derived from the verbal root *div*, which follows many meanings such as playing, desiring victory, and the like.
She is this very one, because she is well-known and experienced by all; [she resides] in your lotus-feet, that is, in your two lotus-like feet.

A particle of the pollen of the dust—that is, a subtle portion—born from that is its "grace" (prasāda), meaning favor. Who is he? He is Udayanapravara Naravāhanadatta, who has become a recipient of your grace because he transcends what is commonly known; for the *Bṛhatkathā* is the source of his story. Even for a ruler of the earth...

The remainder of the sentence is: "Even though he was a ruler of the earth alone, there occurred—meaning, there was obtained—the attainment (*praṇaya*) of the status of a universal emperor (*sārvabhauma*), which is the rank of a *cakravartin*. Of what kind [was he]? He was one who possessed the *vidyādhara* [powers], namely:
sandals, a sword, a *vetāla*, magical substances (*siddhadravya*), and red arsenic (*manaḥśilā*).
"Collyrium, the opening [of the eye], the servant, and likewise the Yakṣiṇī—whatever collection of accomplishments exists within the three worlds.

According to this principle stated in the Vāmakeśvara[tantra], the Vidyādharas are those who uphold the sciences of accomplishment (siddhividyā). Alternatively, they are those who possess knowledge (vidyā).

The *Śikṣā*, *Kalpa*, and the other eighteen [auxiliaries]— those who uphold (*dhara*) these through the accumulation of reading, teaching, and so forth, as well as by practicing their meaning, are the *vidyādharas*, that is, the learned ones; as it is said in the *Vāyavīya Purāṇa*:
The Vedas are four in number, along with Mīmāṃsā, the extensive Nyāya, Purāṇa, and Dharmaśāstra; these indeed are the fourteen branches of knowledge (vidyās).
Āyurveda, Dhanurveda, Gāndharvaveda, and then Arthaśāstra; these are traditionally recorded as the eighteen branches of knowledge (vidyās).

Thus [it is said]. As for those who claim that the *vidyādharas* here are a specific class of gods, that is baseless; for in the present context, the attainment of sovereignty over the *vidyādhara* and *deva* castes is not established. He is one whose footstool—the seat situated beneath his feet—is kissed, that is, touched, by their prostrations and salutations.
The meaning is that having attained sovereignty, he was constantly prostrated at their footstools.

Thus, such is the ripening of grace through contact with the dust of your feet; how much more so when there is the falling of the side-glance of your mercy? This is the intended sense here: [as stated by] Udayanapravara.

A certain king, born of an ordinary family, having attained the status of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) through the grace of Mahādevī, enjoyed the abundance of great enjoyments and sovereignty. The word "api" (even/also) indicates wonder. Here too, the description of the fruit of the worship of Kāmarāja is to be inferred. As for the fruit of the practice (*sādhana*) and so forth of Kāmarāja:
In the Vāmakeśvara [Tantra]:
"Then listen, O Goddess of the Gods!
to the practice of Kāmarāja, as well as the form of Kāmakalā within the sphere of the sprout of Madana."
O Beloved, she has the luster of the rising sun's orb, her body is brilliantly radiant,
she has the form of a flickering lamp-flame, and she pours down a stream of bindus.
She has swallowed up the life-force of the entire expanse of the worlds;
she is the ground of self-identity, established in her own state through the transcendence of her own great majesty.
Then, although she shines forth gradually as far as the bodiless [Ananga] from there,
she is thus one and of a dual nature, extending from the body to the bodiless.

Then, O Goddess of the gods! for those who pride themselves on all their charms and are full of passion, the practitioner, O Goddess, becomes more than a tormentor—he is one whose power exceeds that of the God of Love himself.
Whether it be a woman, a goddess, or even an asura; a vidyādharī, a kinnarī, or a yakṣī; or perhaps a nāga maiden—whosoever comes within the range of his vision.
The daughter of a most fierce king was a perfected maiden (siddhakanyā),
her mind scorched by the fire of the blazing god of love, difficult even for him to behold.
O Goddess! She becomes moist with perspiration, her eyes tremble at the corners, she is bewildered and overwhelmed by passion;
having offered her entire being, she comes completely under one's control.
Resembling the moon reflected in rippling water and reddened by the rays of the rising sun,
she who is meditated upon is instantly consumed within the womb of women.
That very [goddess], having the luster of vermilion, when meditated upon in the heart,
is said to be the attractor of those whose minds are possessed by delusion and infatuation.
Alternatively, when applied to the crown of the head while raining down drops of blood,
it brings the entire world under one's control through the practice of concentration.
Now listen, I shall describe another practice that is difficult to find on earth;
by the mere knowledge of which, the practitioner becomes like the god of love.
One should desire with desire that which abides in desire, stands in the midst of desire, and is enclosed within the womb of desire;
one should desire desire with desire, and cast desire into desires.
Having performed the desired act with desire, one will certainly cause that which abides in desire to tremble.
Thus [it is said]. (7)
Thus, he says that for poets as well, fame— attained through the acquisition of unrestrained, nectar-like utterances of Sarasvatī— is likewise long-lasting,
being the fruit born of your grace: "By those purified by prostration at the dust of your lotus-feet" (an alternative reading is "by the ancients").
By certain meritorious masters of poetry, possessed of no small intellect, fame as white as milk, the moon, silk, or snow has been attained even throughout the three worlds. (8)

O Goddess! By those whose bodies have been purified by the contact of their heads with the dust—the masses of pollen—from your lotus-feet during prostrations, and who are therefore meritorious because they are performers of auspicious deeds consisting of the worship of your feet; for this reason, they are not insignificant—that is, they are not dull-witted.
By those wise ones who possess such minds and intellects— by the learned,

by the poets (*kavayaḥ*) skilled in the composition of poetry and the like, and by certain few among them who have attained the rank of great poet (*mahākavi*) due to their rarity; by these [the work was composed].

By Śrīharṣa, Māgha, Bāṇabhaṭṭa, Kālidāsa, and others throughout the three worlds—even within the triple universe—[the following were surpassed]: milk by the ocean, the moon by the maker of nectar, and silk by fine Chinese cloth. (p. 16) Snow... [is surpassed by... the moon.

In the same way, his fame—his renown—has been obtained as something pure white like snow. Here, by means of many points of comparison based on the collection of numerous white objects, there is an intensification of the quality of whiteness through their combined transformation; thus, by relying on these multiple similes, the preeminence of the quality of incomparable whiteness in his fame is suggested (dhvani). That is to say, [it is implied] by them...

The poets, having composed poems whose very life is the unimpeded flow of the essence of the nectar-ocean of Sarasvatī—attained through the grace of Mahādevī—and which are animated by the aesthetic sentiments (rasas) such as the erotic (śṛṅgāra), have departed to heaven; yet, even now, they live on earth as it were, through their bodies of fame that endure for long. By this, the proclamation of the fruit of the worship of Vāgbhava is indicated.
Thus [ends section] 8.

This indicates that it is not only for humans who depend upon the propitiation of the Goddess for the sake of attaining enjoyments and sovereignty, but even for prosperous gods, so that she may sustain their acquisition and preservation; thus, it serves to produce an excess of the Goddess's favor.
He states the metaphorical means that are not well-known in the world:

"a variegated worship fashioned from the blossoms of the wish-fulfilling tree, accompanied by the sweet songs of his beloved, which have been set ablaze. (Note: *gītim* is an alternative reading for *gītimit*).
O Bhavānī! The Vidyādharas constantly play the lute for you within the cave-dwellings of the Golden Mountain.

O Bhavānī! You bring forth (ānayati), sustain (jīvayati), or illuminate (prakāśa) Bhava—the Great God, the cycle of existence, or desire—because his nature consists of sovereignty that performs what is exceedingly difficult to achieve, and because he is essentially characterized by manifest life.

Or, because her form is the very essence of playful beauty, she is Bhavānī; [this is] her vocative address. In the cave-dwellings—the mountain palaces—of the Golden Mountain (Hemādri), the Vidyādharas, who are a divine race, are constantly and incessantly the possessors (dharāḥ) of the sciences (vidyā) concerning pills, collyrium, swords, sandals, and so forth.

The meaning is that, out of a desire for your favor, these bearers of [the Vedas] delight you with music; they sing near you with lutes (*vīṇā*) in accordance with the proper *tāla* and *laya*, etc., using the *pañcama-grāma* scale and so forth.
This occurs in the presence of the sweet resonance of their sounding lutes.
For in the case of song (p. 17), because the listener’s mind is immersed in the filling of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of extraordinary bliss, an excess of joy arises;
therefore, since they must rely upon the lute as an instrument, [the same applies] there as well.

What more need be said of the music ignited by the indistinct, sweet, and warbling notes of women whose voices are naturally melodious! How wonderful is this [place] fashioned by the blossoms— flowers radiant with fragrance— of the wish-fulfilling trees, such as the Pārijāta and the Saṃtāna!

"Variegated worship" (*citrapūjā*) refers to worship being performed with heaps of flowers of various colors; alternatively, by the word "variegated" (*citra*), various types of ritual services (*upacāra*) are indicated, meaning that worship consists of either five or sixteen services. By this, following the worship—

It has been stated that there is occasion for singing and so forth. To the question "How do they play the lute?", he replies: the songs—belonging to the Vidyādharīs, who are the beloveds of their most dear ones—have been "kindled," meaning brought to brilliance;
they are "red" with the intoxication arising from the joy of drinking divine nectar, and are characterized by sweet vocal melodies.

The phrase "wherein there is a particular composition of musical works (*saṃgītārthaprabandharacanā*) and their arrangement" is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṇa*). As for the *rāgas*, they are well-known in the treatises on music (*saṅgītaśāstra*) by names such as Vasantā, Gūrjarī, Karṇāṭā, and Gauḍī, and they are associated with the seven notes (*svara*), beginning with Ṣaḍja and Madhyama. The mention of the "lute" (*vīṇā*) is illustrative; by it, instruments such as the drum (*mṛdaṅga*) and the flute (*vaṃśa*) are also implied.

Musical instruments are taken up. This is the meaning: at the conclusion of the multicolored worship, the Vidyādharas, together with Vidyādharīs of sweet voice who sing melodiously and flawlessly—possessing the joy of youthful bliss—with their mastery in the arts of the triple symphony (tauryatrika), [perform].
They worship you in their mansions with the playing of lutes, flutes, drums, and other instruments;
by virtue of that greatness, they possess an abundance of superior enjoyments and sovereign power. || 9 ||

Now he extols the fruits of the grace of the Blessed Lady’s feet: O Goddess! May the grace born from Your lotus-feet be victorious—the perfected mantra for the rite of subjugating Lakṣmī, the means for attracting beloved women, and the lamp that utterly pierces the dense darkness of delusion. (10)

O Goddess! [He is] like Lakṣmī in the rite of subjugation regarding wealth, lands, elephants, horses, cattle, and other riches; or like Padmā in the act of subjugation consisting of lifelong obedience; and likewise in the matters of attracting women who are situated at a distance.
Even in the operations of summoning (ākṛṣṭi),
one who has mastered the mantra is successful by means of the five-limbed preliminary service (pañcāṅga-puraścaryā) consisting of prior cultivation (pūrva-sevā).

A mantra—consisting of the nature of reflection (*manana*) and protection (*trāṇa*), and taking the form of a *vidyā* or similar—is one that has been perfected through preliminary recitation (*japa*) numbering one hundred thousand times multiplied by the number of its constituent syllables, and thereby rendered fit for the performance of desired rites according to one's wishes.
The sense is that only a perfected mantra is fit for application, as it brings about the attainment of results without delay. And so it is said:
In the Vāmakeśvara[tantra]:
"Facing that direction, having made one's own body the triple city (tripurīkṛtavigraha),
and having bound the Kṣobhiṇī mudrā, one should recite the Vidyā one hundred and eight times," and so forth.
"One should bring that woman who wanders [in the sky], even from hundreds of leagues"—thus ends [the citation].
Now, what is this "attraction"? Is it of a woman belonging to the practitioner himself, or one belonging to another?
In the first case, since she would already be under his control and situated constantly in his own vicinity, [there would be no need for such a rite].

Because there is no difficulty in accomplishing it and because summoning [the deity] would be purposeless; nor should it be argued that the activity proceeds for the sake of mere curiosity, since curiosity is shown only toward another's woman who resides in the inner apartments and is difficult to attain; and in the second case [if it were a duty], it would be untenable because unrighteousness (*adharma*) is not enjoined by scriptural injunction (*vidhi*). Therefore:

The efficacy of the prescriptive injunctions would lie in the difficulty of accomplishment when [the act] is performed through forceful abduction or similar means against one's own unwilling wife; and there exists a historical account in the *Pīṭhamāhātmyas* concerning how the wife of the sage named Nārāyaṇa, called Candravadanā, was taken by the son of Śakti.

The sage recovered the Goddess who had been abducted by Seturāja only after propitiating her; or else, one must assume another result for the attraction of another's wife that does not contradict dharma. Or, even if the attraction were indeed for the sake of sexual enjoyment, it still cannot be considered a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*), because its connection [to the rite] is established solely through the process of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*). As it has been stated in the *Tantravārtika*:
Furthermore, the cognition regarding the cultivation of the constituent parts of the fruit is highly prescriptive;
Jaimini will state this here, [asserting] that its desire for attainment is characterized by its purpose.

And because there is an absence of scriptural injunction (*vihitatva*) in this case, the desire for another's wife does not constitute unrighteousness (*adharma*); however, in the performance under discussion which serves as the means for that [desire], there is indeed righteousness (*dharma*), just as in the case of the Śyena sacrifice. As for those passages written by the authors of the *Śyāmārahasya*, such as "the Kaulika is the husband of all women," according to the method of extracting their true meaning:

"The nature of the Dharma (dharmatva) must be understood solely from the mouth of the Guru," so say the venerable Śrī Bhāskararāya. Likewise, it is a lamp that pierces— that is, cuts through and tears asunder— the dense, thick darkness of delusion, which consists of a lack of discernment.
Because it removes ignorance, it is preeminent; it is an illuminator like a lamp.
Just as a lamp dispels darkness, so too is this grace of yours.

The meaning is that it effects the destruction of ignorance, which is the cause of sinking into the ocean of saṃsāra. Alternatively, it is a "lamp" (pradīpa) because it shines intensely in the sky or illuminates all worldly objects; such a sun, which removes the darkness of delusion, is "born from your feet," meaning produced by your two lotus-feet.
Grace, which is favor, triumphs; it exists as one ever more capable of bestowing excellent fruits that excel each other in degree.
As it has been said:
"It brings about misfortune [to others], while this [grace] becomes a wonderful abode consisting of the locus of supreme bliss and awakening."
Seated upon a couch laden with abundant gold, O Mother, you bring about either grace or wrath, whereby one crosses over all difficulties.
In this context, regarding the interpretation of favor (*prasāda*), the word division is *asau iti*. "Gold" (*kārtasvaram*) means its own color; "bed" (*palyaṅkaḥ*) means a couch;

"crossing the forest" (*kāntārasya taraṇam*). But in the interpretation of anger (*kopa*), *asaubhāgyam* is a single word. The word division is *ayam iti*. "Variegated" (*vicitram*) means devoid of pictures (*vigata-citram*); "the cry of distress of the children" (*pṛthukānām ārtasvaraḥ*); "on the lap of the wife" (*palyā aṅke*) refers to the pleasure of the beloved.

The word *raṇam* is to be applied here through punning (*śleṣa*). Thus, it is stated that for those graced by the favor of having attained Your feet, both worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*) are easily obtained without restraint.
Such a state occurs only for a few rare individuals who are devoted to the worship of the lotus-feet of Śrī Sundarī.
Blessed are those for whom it is said:
"Where there is enjoyment, there is no liberation; where there is liberation, there is no enjoyment.
But for those intent on the worship of Śrīsundarī, both enjoyment and liberation are held within the palm of their hand."
In this context, it should be inferred that the primary intention is to specifically describe the excellence of the fruit resulting from the worship of the *kūṭas* of the Śrīvidyā. || 10 ||

Even the women of heaven, hoping for the grace of your feet, say with this intention: "O Goddess, the rays from the ground of the jewels of your toenails, possessing the luster of fresh pearls, bring forth joy."
(20) Those [rays] which, in the course of their service and attendance upon the celestial beauties, have become like clusters of flowers upon the parting line of their hair.

O Goddess! Your toe-nails—the nails on your feet—are themselves jewels; or rather, they are rays (mayūkha) produced from those jewels, originating from the earth as their source, which are like fresh pearls. These rays are the red luster of your toenails. They are [like] fresh pearls.
Those whose luster is a white radiance like that of pearls,

and who for this very reason carry and cause to blossom in the hearts of devotees— those longing to behold their lotus feet— an abundance of joy and bliss; [they are so] during service, at the time of attendance, and in the act of prostration.

The meaning is that in the hair-tufts of the celestial beauties, the lovely women of the gods, who were occupied in prostrating at his feet, there appeared— on the boundary, that is, the edge of their partings— a cluster of flowers acting like a bouquet of blossoms,
having become like a bunch of flower-stalks within their masses of hair.

For it is the custom of beautiful women to wear flowers; since the tresses of the celestial nymphs are dark in color, the rays of their nails—being white—are transformed there into the form of flower clusters (*stabaka*). "Clusters" refers to buds on the verge of blossoming. (11)
Now, ascertaining through direct perception that the power of energy (*śaktitejas*) has transformed in three ways according to its specific locations,

he illuminates his own conviction of self-recognition (*pratyabhijñā*): "Blazing with the brilliance of the shimmering moon upon the crown, the middle of the forehead is variegated by the rays of the weapon [the trident] held in the center."
O Mother! This light which kisses the heart-center and corresponds to the minute spark of the sacrificial fire—that is your true nature.
"O Mother! This is the Light—the light of lights, which the gods worship as life and immortality"—thus says the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (4.4.16). This is the Supreme Śākta [Light].

It is that by which the sun shines, as established in the Śruti and Smṛti: "The sun does not shine there" (Kaṭhopaniṣad 5.15), "The sun does not illuminate it" (Bhagavadgītā 15.6), and "By whose light the sun burns, being kindled with splendor.
It is the Supreme.
(On page 21:

Because of the usage in such Vedic passages as "having attained the light" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.3.4) and "may he enjoy the light of the mind" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā), its status as the Supreme is declared, since it has the nature of illumination. That is your own.

Form is unique; this form is to be personally experienced. To the question "What is it?", he says: that which, from the crown of the head—that is, from the *ājñācakra* up to the *brahmabila*—is shimmering and blossoming, radiant and beautiful like the light of the cool-rayed moon, the moonlight.

Because it causes delight to the heart, pacifies burning heat, and brings joy to the eyes, it is likewise [compared] to the weapon of Indra (the rainbow) situated between the forehead and the *ājñācakra*— that is to say, from the *ādhāra* up to the heart,
reaching the *hṛccakra*, it is a spark of the fire-god Agni.

Just as [tiny sparks], so too [is it] corresponding and resembling that; even with the reading *anukārī*, the meaning is "similar. The word "shines" (*bhāti*) is to be supplied. This is the intended sense:
for practitioners, that very form of light in the shape of a shimmering star situated in the *mūlādhāra* appears likewise in the three locations.

Thus, that which appears in such variety should be cultivated. As it has been said: "O Great Goddess, Your light shines like a mass of gold in the womb [of the body], like a flash of lightning in the heart, and like the moon in the Ājñā [cakra]."

Thus, by this, the locations, phonemes, and meditations for the three seeds of the ignorance of the ignorant are also indicated. This has been demonstrated in detail in the first verse of the First Praise. || 12 ||
Now he introduces a specific meditation on Kāmeśvarī that is conducive to subjugation:

"O Mṛḍānī, O Tripurā! He who, casting aside shame, beholds you even for a moment—[you] who seem to smear the sky with a mass of vermilion dust, or to bathe the earth in liquid lacquer through your own splendor—"
Those of good vision run after him. || 13 ||

O Tripurā! The etymological derivation of the word *Tripurā* should be understood as "she who existed prior to the three cities," and so forth. Furthermore, the city or capital of the triad consisting of the knower (*mātṛ*), the means of knowledge (*māna*), and the object of knowledge (*meyā*) is Śrī Lalitāmbā;
she is called *Tripurā* because she existed prior to the three forms (*mūrti*). As it has been said:
Because the triad of forms is also ancient, the name of their Mother is Tripurā; as Gauḍapāda said (p.

The phrase "is divided by the three principles" (tattvatrayeṇābhidyate) means that Brahman, which is indeed one, is divided by the three principles. The term *tattva* has been explained in many ways—as the qualities (*guṇa*), the forms (*mūrti*), the seeds (*bīja*), the worlds (*jagat*), the seats (*pīṭha*), the sections (*khaṇḍa*), and so forth; thus, the meaning here is "from the cities [consisting of] the qualities and so on. In the *Kālikā Purāṇa*, however, having introduced the passage beginning with "And her mandala is a triangle," etc., [it continues as follows].

"Since each triad is threefold, therefore that is considered Tripurā. This has also been stated by the venerable Ācārya himself in the verse beginning with "The triad of the gods, the triad of the Vedas, the triad of the fires," and so forth.
By your splendor—that is, by the ruddy luster arising from your body—the sky (dyām), the ether (vyoma), [is filled] with the dust of vermilion (sindūra-pāṃsūnām).

He who, even for a moment during the time of meditation— meaning, he who meditates upon— the earth (the world) as if it were strewn, inlaid, and colored by masses and heaps of vermilion powder, or as if it were bathed and drenched in liquid lac; his mind is permeated by the contemplation of You.

O Mṛḍānī! Abandoning bashfulness and shame—such as that arising from the transgression of boundaries through slander of others—the beautiful-eyed women, those with deer-like eyes, pursue and run after the devotee who is absorbed in meditation. As it is said in the *Saundaryalaharī*: [The verse follows: "O Goddess, the deer-eyed women, having cast aside modesty and shame born of the fear of public censure, run after the one who meditates upon You. (Note: The specific verse from the *Saundaryalaharī* is not provided in the source text, but the commentary explains its meaning.)
"By the shadows of your body, which follow the path of the splendor of the newly risen sun," and so forth. Here, by the phrase "by your brilliance" (*tvattejasā*), redness (*lauhitya*) is suggested.
And this redness is *vimarśa* (reflective awareness); as it is stated in the *Kādimata*:
"One's own self alone is declared to be the deity, Lalitā, whose form is the universe."
That redness is its reflective awareness; this is "upāsti" (worship), which is to say, it is *bhāvanā* (contemplative cultivation).
Thus it is said. Also in the Vāmakeśvara [Tantra]:
"The Goddess Tripurā herself is indeed Lauhitya, which is its reflective awareness (vimarśana).
This refers to the venerable Mahātripurasundarī, whose nature consists of the state of equilibrium between the aforementioned Light (prakāśa) and Reflective Awareness (vimarśa).
Meditation (*dhyāna*) possesses a threefold nature by way of being gross, subtle, and supreme. Among these, that which is distinguished by [features such as] the head, hands, and feet is gross;
that consisting of mantra is subtle; while the supreme consists of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) or pure consciousness (*saṃvit*).
As it is said in the *Yogavāsiṣṭha*:
O sinless one, know that my two forms are the supreme universal;
while the ignorant worship that universal form which is endowed with hands and other limbs.
"The supreme form of mine, which is without beginning or end, unique and free from affliction—this is expressed by such terms as Brahman, Ātman, and Paramātman.
"Generality is said to be twofold, through the distinction between the gross and the subtle.
Thus it is stated in the *Jñānārṇava*, in the discussion on optional ritual applications (*kāmyaprayoga*):
"The three worlds are filled with the mass of the sindūra of her splendor."
O Supreme Goddess! one should meditate [upon her], and she shall delude the three worlds in an instant.
O Queen of the Gods! Just as Kandarpa is the destroyer of the pride of women, so do kings, serpents, rākṣasas, and gods fall under her control.
"By meditating upon her with the mind, a woman shall become submissive like a maidservant.
Thus, by means of the meditation on Kāmeśvarī, the fruit of the worship of the *kūṭa* of Kāmarāja is indicated.
Even when those who follow that path, who partake in the *kulācāra*, and who possess keen vision, transgress the bounds of social restraint (*maryādā*), [the result is as described].

Because the attainment of happiness both here and in the hereafter occurs through the power of family-initiation (kuladīkṣā) and the resulting state of being free from bondage, the address "O Mṛḍānī" is made with specific intention. || 13 ||
Now, he elaborates upon meditation along with its fruit by way of another method:
"He who remembers your true form—even for a single moment—[seeing it] like a thread spreading through lac-dye, becomes [liberated];
those scorched by the god of love meditate upon him with undistracted minds."
Young women [perceive] the quality of loveliness at the limit of Pradyumna. || 14 ||
O Mother!

He who meditates—even for a moment, even for two *ghaṭikās*—upon your own form, which resembles a thread of lac, originating from the flow of liquid lac; [he who meditates thus] is one tormented by the bodiless god, afflicted by the fever of passion.
Young women, whose minds were fixed on no other and whose conduct was directed toward none else,
meditated upon his true nature— which resembled a thread of red lac dye— and [perceived] the quality of supreme beauty within the very limits of Pradyumna, the god of love.

They meditate upon him who possesses the quality of good fortune; the meaning is that they contemplate in their hearts one who is indistinguishable from Kāma in beauty and who brings about the subsiding of the fever of desire. As before, here too, both the method of worship and its fruit are to be understood. || 14 ||
24) He describes the aforementioned meditation, along with its method, by means of another formulation:
"By the power of restraining the foundational breath (ādhāra-māruta), those [who practice] possess [a light] resembling the qualities of a lotus dyed with vermilion."
O Goddess! Your radiant form throbs within the heart; those who meditate upon it here attain the accomplishment of their desired goals. || 15 ||

O Goddess! In the hearts of those who are intent on the sport of creating the universe, or whose true essence is luminosity and so forth, Your body—in the form of Śaktikuṇḍalinī, the partless (niṣkala) essential nature known as Kāmakalā—shines and manifests within the region of the Unstruck Sound (anāhata). Of what sort is it? [It is that] which, in the Ādhāra—the Mūlādhāra-cakra—is of the nature of wind.
By means of the restraint of the vital air consisting of prāṇa and apāna, according to the method taught by the Guru, and preceded by the arousal of the *śakti*,

the lotus-stalk [of the central channel]— which is ignited and possesses a throbbing light through the practice of the movement of the fire-*kuṇḍalinī* ascending by way of the *suṣumṇā* via the upward exhalation (*ūrdhvarecaka*)— is therefore colored red, as if dyed with vermilion.

The "bisatantu" (lotus-fiber) follows that [central channel] and is similar to it; from the *mūlādhāra* up to the heart, it resembles the filament of a red lotus and is as radiant as ten million flashes of lightning—this is the meaning. Here, in this world, among desired objects consisting of both worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*), the "siddha" is the goal (*upeya*) already attained, while the "sādhya" is the object yet to be reached.

By this, it is implied by the sense that those for whom their desired goals (*sādhyas*) have been accomplished— even though they are free from desire (*niṣkāma*)— meditate [upon Him], how much more so those who possess desire? Furthermore, they are such as those whose "desired" (*samīhita*)— meaning cherished mental longings (*manoratha*) consisting of the ultimate reality of both enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*)— have been "accomplished" (*siddha*), that is, brought to fulfillment.
The deities known as the Sādhyas meditate upon and remember [them]; this is a restatement of the meditation previously described as "sindūra" and so forth. || 15 ||
He describes the previously mentioned meditation as fruitful by way of its being situated within the solar disc:
"O Mother! those who contemplate Your form, tawny like fresh lac-paste, residing in the center of the crimson orb..."
Their chests are always pierced by the arrows of the flower-armed god, and thus those fawn-eyed women remain under their control. || 16 ||
O Mother! That form of yours which is as tawny as the mud of thick liquid lac, like fresh alaktaka dye— (p.
[The deity] is red-colored and resides in the center of the ruddy orb; because it is to be meditated upon there, as the Śruti states:

"This golden person who is seen within the sun" (Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad 10.1), and because this has been established in the *Antarādhikaraṇa*. Furthermore, they constantly contemplate [the deity] as residing in the solar Kuṇḍalinī.

They remember those deer-eyed women whose chests and hearts were pierced by the arrows of the flower-armed god; by this, it is understood that their eyes possess a similarity in qualities such as clarity, loveliness, and expansiveness. They have come under his control.
They become dependent; the meaning is that they serve [the deity] throughout their entire lives by means of the gift of all possessions and so forth.
Thus, the fruit of worshipping Kāmeśvarī, the presiding deity of the middle *kūṭa*, among these two aforementioned verses, should be inferred. || 16 ||
Now, he describes the meditation on Vāgīśvarī together with its fruit:
"O Goddess of Speech, for one who beholds in their mind your form, white as the shimmering rays of the moon,
words sweet with grace flow forth from them— a boundless cascade of the nectar of well-composed hymns."

"O Goddess," as before; "your form" consists of the presiding deity of speech (*vāg-adhidevatā*), composed of the presiding principle of the *vāk-kūṭa*, having Vāgīśvarī as its essence; it is as white and radiant as the shimmering rays of the moon—the cool-beamed lunar rays—[shining] upon the mind, the heart, [or the head].

"Ālokate" means he beholds, sees, or meditates upon. The reading "śirasi" (on the head) is more appropriate, because in the first hymn, it was stated, "Those who [meditate on] you as the white lotus...";
thus, by virtue of the similarity with the meditation on Vāgīśvarī, it should be understood that she is to be meditated upon specifically in the location of the head.

Of him who has emerged beyond the boundary or from the boundary— being limitless and boundless— and whose [speech] is a fountain of nectar consisting of well-composed verses and a collection of elegant sayings, which,
by virtue of producing excellence in coolness and refreshment, is a flow of the essence of ambrosia.
The words— meaning the goddesses of speech (Bhāratīs)— belonging to one who has obtained your grace, which consists of the mastery of speech,
flow forth from the mouth, issuing out both sweet through the quality of clarity known as *prasāda* in literary composition, and charming, being endowed with sweetness (*mādhurya*).
The meaning is that the poet becomes one whose speech is sweet with the flowing nectar of well-spoken verses.
Furthermore, the fruit of the practice of the *vāgbhava-kūṭa* is described in the *Vāmakeśvaratantra* (p.
O Goddess of gods! Listen now to the method for accomplishing this Vāgbhava [which consists of the triad of seed-syllables]:
clad in white garments and standing amidst white garments, one should practice.
A man devoted to celibacy should worship with white flowers and with white food offerings, such as curd,
milk, boiled rice, and so forth.
O Supreme Goddess! having worshipped her with white flowers of pure resolve— which grant fruits according to one's desire— one should meditate upon the supreme Vāgīśvarī.

Then, having pierced the knot of Brahmā at the tip of the tongue, one should contemplate her in the form of a lamp, shining as a seed-syllable up to the station of Anaṅga, awakening consciousness and bliss.
One whose heart is ruined, who is vulgar, foolish, a great sinner,
or even a rogue— such a person is unable to speak even a single word clearly, with distinct syllables.
Though he be dull-witted, mute, of extremely poor intellect, devoid of wisdom, or ruined in mind,
even he becomes eloquent like another Vācaspati.
He was a conqueror of the haughty assemblies of true scholars, possessed of unimpeded brilliance,
and a connoisseur of the essence of sound reasoning, the meaning of words and sentences, and the ornaments of poetry— the six systems of philosophy.
One should compare it to the garlands of waves in the ocean tossed by the wind;
preceded by extremely delicate, expansive meters and poetic ornaments, and characterized by [the quality of] *rīti*.
O Goddess, by means of the composition of verses, one becomes a creator of great epics (mahākāvya) and one who has reached the further shore of the knowledge of the Vedas,
the Vedāṅgas, and the established tenets of Vedānta.
He was a knower of the words of the Mīmāṃsā, the Smṛtis, and the histories such as the Jyotiḥśāstra;
he was a knower of many mantras from the Purāṇas, the Rasas, the Vādās, and the Gāruḍa.
He was a knower of the true meaning of the Pātālaśāstra, the Vijñānabhūta-tantra, and other scriptures;
he was highly skilled in various arts, such as painting and diverse crafts.
Possessing all speech refined by the noble sounds of the great prophecy,
he understands the knowledge of all languages and dialects and is skilled in all forms of writing.

A knower of the study of the meanings of various treatises, renowned for his knowledge of the arts and the Vedas along with their auxiliary sciences (vedāṅgas), he was famous throughout the world. (p.
27) [Note: "iti" refers to alternative readings found in the Kāśī edition.]
"O Goddess! One becomes a knower of all speech and omniscient. (4-21-33).
Thus [ends the section]. 17.
Now, anticipating the objection, "But why this repeated description of you?", he praises her while illuminating his own intended meaning by mentioning a common attribute:
"O Śarvāṇī! O you whose lotus-feet are worshipped by all people! O you whose splendor of eyes mocks the beauty of a lotus petal!"
O royal swan of the minds of people whose forms are free from sin! You destroy the manifold calamities of mankind. (18)

She is called Śarvāṇī because she "shatters" (śṛṇāti) and destroys the mass of the impurities of ignorance; thus, "O Śarvāṇī! means O Dispeller of the Darkness of Ignorance! Furthermore, "O You whose lotus-feet (padma-pādau) are saluted and bowed to by all people—by all living beings who fear birth and death!"
O you whose lotus-feet are worshipped by all people! This is an address [to her] because she possesses such exquisite beauty.

The intention is that she is the remover of the fear of death. O you whose splendor of the eyes—the beauty of the eyes—is imitated or compared to the *chavi* (luster) of lotus petals—that is, the leaves of the water-lily! This is an address [to her].

O you whose splendor of the eyes mocks the beauty of the lotus petals! O you with lovely eyes as broad as lotus leaves! The meaning is that you bestow joy by raining down a shower of the nectar of your own gaze; likewise, in the minds of those people worthy of grace—those whose bodies and forms are stainless and from whom all impurity has vanished.

The meaning is that she dwells, constantly manifesting within the hearts of those she favors to grace, just as a royal swan joyfully sports and resides in Lake Mānasa; or alternatively, she shines resplendent in the minds of those whose actions are solely pure.
The meaning is that she is of the nature of the *haṃsa*-color, of the nature of the *ajapā* mantra, or of the nature of the *haṃsa* mantra. As it is said in the *Śrīvidyārṇava*:
"O Goddess, O sinless one, I shall describe to you the worship of the *ajapā*."
For whom, by mere realization, the Supreme Brahman itself becomes the teacher.
O Supreme Goddess! If a man bound by delusion chants the *haṃsapada* mantra every day, he does not realize it; for him, there is no liberation.
O Goddess, when [the mantra] is known and recited through the grace of the glorious Guru,
then, by means of the inhalation and exhalation, the destruction of bondage occurs.
In inhalation and exhalation, there are the two syllables "haṃsa.
Therefore, the vital breath (prāṇa), known as Haṃsa, abides in the form of the Self (ātman).
Six breaths constitute one *prāṇa*; sixty of those are considered a *nāḍikā*.
Sixty *nāḍikās* make up a day and night; this is the count for the recitation (*japa*) of the mantra.
O Īśvarī, every living being recites twenty-one thousand six hundred times daily the supreme mantra consisting of vibration and bliss.
Its birth is the commencement, and its death is the offering;
O Goddess of the gods, even without formal recitation, the mantra-practitioner’s recitation becomes perfected.
Therefore, O Goddess, it is called Ajapeya, which severs the bonds of worldly existence; it is obtained, O Beloved, through the grace of the venerable Guru and not otherwise.
O Maheśānī! Having thus performed the recitation, one should offer it daily to Gaṇeśa, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara, O Parameśvarī.
One should offer six thousand [verses] to the individual soul (jīvātman), then likewise one thousand to the supreme soul (paramātman),
then another thousand to the Guru, offering them in this sequential order.
Having reported that recitation performed during that day and night, O beloved,
O wise one, perform the innate placement (*nyāsa*), O Supreme Goddess.
The sage is Haṃsa; the meter is said to be Gāyatrī, which was unmanifest in the beginning;
the deity is the Supreme Source; and Haṃsa is said to be the seed-syllable *Haṃ*.
He is Śakti, He is Kīlaka, He is Aham, and He is indeed Praṇava, the very principle itself;
likewise, O Supreme Goddess, He is the station of Nāda and the color white.
The accent known as udātta is thus proclaimed to belong to this mantra;
know this, O Pārvatī, that its application is for the sake of liberation.
Then, for the purification of the body, one should perform the placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa);
O Goddess, [one should place] Sūrya, Soma, and thereafter Nirañjana.
One should sequentially assign the [mantras] ending in *svāhā* and preceded by *nirābhāsa*;
having assigned those ending in *kavaca*, one should then contemplate the state of the infinite (*ananta*).
Having uttered the four subtle forms (*tanusūkṣma*) ending in the neuter suffix *ṅ*,
one should impel [the mantra] with *svāhā* at the end, preceded by the unmanifest word (*avyaktapada*).
The mantra whose nature is awakening, ending with the wife of the fire (svāhā) in the fourth position, is declared to be the weapon (astra).
O Goddess of gods! the two wings of this swan are the Nigama and Āgama.
Agni and Soma are the two wings, while Tāra is the head;
the three Bindus are the crest-lock, Nāda is established in the eyes and the mouth.
The pair of feet of Śiva and Śakti, with Kālāgni as their twin flanks—
this Supreme Swan (Paramahaṃsa) is all-pervading and luminous.
Resembling ten million suns, he shines by his own radiance;
this Haṃsa, whose nature is withdrawal, also reveals discernment.

"The Gāyatrī known as Ajapā is difficult to obtain in the three worlds. Thus, you destroy—that is, you remove—the manifold calamities, such as birth and other fears, afflictions, and poverty, for people who offer salutations and the like; therefore, please dispel those [calamities] for me as well.
The prayer is implied. || 18 ||
Now, one might object: "Since Paramaśiva alone is capable of accomplishing all desired objects, he is the one who should be prayed to.
Anticipating this, [the author] says with the intention that even his such status is well-known only through your power:
"O Saṃkarṣiṇī! Having approached him, you [bestow] excellence of qualities in accordance with his desire."
[“Having touched” is an alternative reading.
When you wear it, then even the god Śiva—the sole preceptor of the three worlds and the architect of the three realms—would be born. 19.
O Saṃkarṣiṇī! O thou who manifestest the supreme Bhairava as being under thy own control! O Kālasaṃkarṣiṇī!

O Supreme Śakti! [Bestow] that excellence—the pre-eminence (*prakarpa*) of the qualities (*guṇas*), such as *sattva* and the rest—which is appropriate (*anurūpa*), meaning conforming to each respective object, and which accords with the desire regarding the objects of seeking, knowing, and acting, in accordance with one's will.
Having touched [it] with your hand, you then, by facing toward it, cause your own self to manifest and expand;
when you thus sustain or maintain it— or rather, assume a form according to your will, that is to say, in accordance with the will of Śiva— [then you bestow grace].

That [state] in which there is a preeminence— an excellence of gradation— of the multitude of qualities such as omniscience and the like, which appear as appropriate to their respective states of Sadāśiva and so forth, by means of the non-abandonment of the state of the subjects ranging from Śiva down to the Sakala, who have not yet attained the assumption of those respective specific classes [of subjects].
"Having approached" means "having accepted. As it has been said:
"O Mother of the World! You are victorious, for Time, in the form of Bhairava, creates the universe from the immovable [mountains] down to the smallest insect, by the power of Your will."

At that time, the renowned Śiva, whose essence is Kāmeśvara, was the sole preeminent Guru in the three worlds— including the realms of existence and non-existence— the director of the universe's activities and the divine instructor,
characterized by the play of manifesting and sustaining the wondrous drama of the world filled with manifold aesthetic sentiments.

You alone would become the creator of the three worlds, like a stage director; for you alone perform the task of creating the universe and so forth, since without you it would be incapable of acting. Just as a certain stage director [produces] a drama filled with the sweetness of sentiments such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and containing excellent seeds and other elements...

Just as a dancer, possessing the skill to present to the audience the offering of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*)— which is to be manifested through various enacted roles and directly realized— attains the status of a master of drama (*nāṭyācārya*) and the title of *sūtradhāra* in the world after introducing the performance for the spectators to relish that flavor; in the same way, Śiva, desiring to engage in the cosmic play, becomes you alone.
The meaning is that she initiates the drama of the three worlds by means of her most praiseworthy form. Furthermore, within the Trika system,
according to the sequence of the emergence of Sṛṣṭikālī and the others in the ritual procedure of Śākta sacrifice, she who is the ultimate Mahākālī—
known as the supreme Pārameśvarī described as Mahābhairava-caṇḍograghorakālī— is indeed that very one.

She is called Kālasaṃkarṣiṇī. As it is said in the *Śrīkramastotra*: "I bow to Mahābhairavaghoracaṇḍakālī, whose splendor is like the moon in the sky of the *kalās*, and whose supreme existence consists of the skillful movement through the wheels of rays belonging to the three sequences (*krama*)."
Thus it is said; and elsewhere:
"Even at the level of the venerable Sadāśiva, the most fierce Kālī, with her terrifyingly arched brows, will become the ground of defeat.
Having thus reflected and attained the supreme state, one should forcefully abide in the Goddess Kālasaṃkarṣiṇī.

Thus, or rather, she is called Saṃkarṣiṇī because Time—which consists of the pentad beginning with Prāṇa—manifests through its internal and external forms. And so the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta says:
"At the tip of the nose, Kālasaṃkarṣiṇī is always present as the threefold Time."
Situated in the mouth, it draws [the breath] into the heart during the movement of inhalation and exhalation.
Through inhalations and breath-retentions she sustains [the world], but through exhalation she devours it;
rising in an instant by means of exhalation, she devours all of time.
