The supreme power of will, known by the name Parā, is that which, in awakening the triad of powers,
performs the sacrifice and draws forth everything that shatters the support of time.
Thus, the venerable Jayaratha explains this: here indeed, the Blessed Goddess Kālasaṃkarṣiṇī, residing in the mouth,

is always present through the synthesis of the inhalation and exhalation that constitute the two lateral channels, within the heart at the central abode and at the tip of the power of the nose, characterized by the threefold [breaths] of prāṇa, apāna, and udāna.

She draws forth time and, by means of various forms, causes it to circulate; for she withdraws it through *recaka* (exhalation), grants entry through *pūraka* (inhalation), and holds it steady through *kumbhaka* (retention). Having arisen by means of the upward *recaka* through the sequence of transcending each respective causal state, she [destroys] all time in an instant.

She withdraws [all things] by means of the process of reducing them to their own essential nature (svarūpa), which is indeed perfectly undivided. By the statement "the first moment (truṭi) of Her will," this supreme Will-power (icchā-śakti) is indicated;
She is to be worshipped under the name Kālasaṃkarṣiṇī, as introduced above, who is the ground of origin for the triad of powers whose essence is Will and the rest.

The meaning is that she draws forth this wind—the support of time—which consists of the entire pentad beginning with *prāṇa*, by making it manifest both internally and externally. As it is said in the *Yāmala*:
"This gross time moves along two paths for yogins."
Adorned with the three powers in the left, the right, and the middle.
"She shall swallow the threefold time as Kālasaṃkarṣiṇī. Thus,
by the name Kālasaṃkarṣiṇī, she performs the drawing back (*saṃkarṣaṇa*) of time— which resides within the cavity of the mouth—
into the heart during the movement of inhalation and exhalation.
"One should retain [the breath] on all sides by means of inhalation (pūraka) and retention (kumbhaka);
the Goddess, arisen through exhalation (recaka), devours time in an instant. Thus it is said.
The supreme power of will, known by the name Parā, is invoked for the awakening of the triad of powers; she draws forth everything that shatters the support of time.
Or rather, the Goddess Kālasaṃkarṣiṇī, who is renowned as the Anākhyā (the Ineffable) in the Uttarāmnāya,
is worshipped in the four Āmnāyas during the ritual adoration of Śrīvidyā. Therefore,
because she herself is not delimited by time, she would be inexpressible even by conceptual constructs such as "eternity" and the like.

As the teacher Utpaladeva said: "That wherein there is no cognition of time—neither 'always,' nor 'then,' nor even 'at one time'—this is Your vision; it is neither eternal, nor can it be described otherwise. (Utpaladeva-stotra 12)
"Thus the Knower, the time of time, the possessor of qualities, the all-knowing"—so says the Śruti (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.2). || 19 ||
Now, with the intention of demonstrating the majesty of the Goddess, he extends [her] nature as Śakti to other things as well:
"This moon, which shines as a jewel in the ocean of the sky; this ancient Puruṣa, who is the teacher of gods and demons;"
"O Goddess! You alone are that beautiful left half of this slayer of Andhaka"—thus they declare. || 20 ||

O Goddess! This moon, which shines and blazes as the nectar-rayed one situated within that very ocean of the sky—the mine of jewels—is you yourself, because it is merely a fraction of the luster of your smile.
As it has been said by the Teachers:
"O Mother! The sun, garlanded with rays, is but a speck to your eyes; the moon is but a drop of your gentle smile.
Here, due to the similarity of being unfathomable depth and so forth, the sky is superimposed as an ocean (*arṇava*);
and due to its quality of providing delight and its whiteness, the moon is superimposed as a jewel (*ratna*). And this [jewel] which belongs to the gods and demons...
You alone are the ancient Puruṣa, the venerable teacher of the gods and the Dānavas, the creator Brahmā; or else, you are even Viṣṇu, the Ancient Puruṣa.
Since she too is of your nature, so it is said in the *Harivaṃśa* by Nārada:
"The illustrious goddess Umā is the first portion of Prakṛti;
Viṣṇu, the creator of the worlds, who is manifest and consists of all things, is designated as female."

Thus [it is said]. And as for that left half of Śiva—the slayer of Andhaka, the enemy of the Asura named Andhaka—which, due to his being Ardhanārīśvara, is the right side; the wise declare and maintain that all of that is you alone—this is the implied meaning. This is the literal sense. But in reality:

The manifestation of the mass of rays within the three wheels situated in front, due to their being composed of Soma, Sūrya, and Agni, is to be understood as the majesty of You alone; thus should this extremely secret meaning be known. || 20 ||
Now, he repeats the meditation on Vāgīśvarī for the purpose of generating the flow of speech:
"O Haimavatī! You are the one meditated upon by that stainless-minded person whose radiance is as pure as the garland of rays of the moon;
O beautiful one, you create for him a play of speech—unimpeded, faultless, and enduring for infinite aeons—in just a few days. (21)
"O Haimavati!"—this is an address meaning "the daughter of Himavat," O daughter of the Himālayas; or else, "O Umā, who belongs to Himavat.

As it is stated in the commentary on the *Kenopaniṣad*: "Umā is Haimavatī. Alternatively, it refers to one who possesses *haimāni* ornaments—that is, those made of gold (*heman*). [She whose] mind (*mānasa*) is stainless and pure...
By that one whose mind is stainless— that devoted person whose radiance and luster are pure and white like the garland of rays of the cool-rayed moon (Himāṃśu),
[the goddess] who sprinkles cool nectar and is therefore white in color; for this very reason, she is called Haimavatī because she originates from the Himavat mountain.
The address is intentional: "You are perceived as such a meditator. O beautiful one!

O you of enviable fortune! In a few days, before long, without delay, unswerving, irreproachable, free from defects such as harshness to the ear, endowed with a multitude of qualities such as clarity, and lasting for infinite eons—[he will attain that].
Alternatively, "end" (*anta*) means termination; because that is absent, it is "infinite" (*ananta*). The suffix *-kalpa* is used here in the sense of "not quite complete.
Thus, [the phrase] *anantakalpam* refers to the play of words (*vācām*), that is, of speech (*girām*), which remains incomplete.

You create and bring forth the flow of poetry overflowing with diverse sentiments; this too is to be understood as resulting from the intention of meditating upon the Goddess of Speech (Vāgīśvarī). || 21 ||

Now, establishing the Goddess through various names that follow the meanings of diverse traditions, he says: "O Goddess! They praise You as Vyāpinī, as Samanā, as Kuṇḍalī; they praise You as Kāminī, as Kamalā, as Kalāvatī;
they praise You as Mālinī, as Lalitā, as Aparājitā, as Vijayā, as Jayā, and as Umā. (22)

The supreme, subtle power of Śiva known as *icchā* (Will), having transcended the mind, is called *unmanā*; it is non-different from the nature of Śiva due to its unconditioned, self-luminous radiance. When that very power agitates the Self—which is of the nature of the Great Being consisting of Light—so that it can no longer endure its state of total non-extension (*asūtraṇa*).

When it manifests as the thread that strings together the entire universe, from the void (*śūnya*) and the absolute void (*atiśūnya*) down to the earth (*dharā*), having ascended to the state of the supreme subject (*parapramātṛ*), it is called the power named *Samanā*, because it consists of the entirety of the objects of thought and the acts of thinking thus strung together. This very power, *Samanā*, while manifesting as if it were the first act of delineation (*ullekha*),...

When it encompasses the entire universe as its object of manifestation—encompassment being its appearing as one with its own self—it is then called the Pervasive One (*vyāpinī*), whose nature is the Void beyond the void (*śūnyātiśūnyātmā*). When that very [power] is oriented toward expansion, by immersing itself in its non-dual nature, it manifests the "this-ness" (*idantā*) of the object through the appearance of the void; at that time:
The great power known as Kuṇḍalinī is so called because she contains within her womb the entire expanse of the universe, including its creation and dissolution;
she is designated as the "Upper Kuṇḍalinī" (ūrdhvakuṇḍalinī) because the entire universe remains unmanifested and held within her interior.
One should not be deluded into thinking that the *mūlakuṇḍalinī* is located here below;

rather, due to its association with the *vyāpinī* and others, it should be understood as the state of the Great Power (*mahāśakti*), the fourth level (*turīya*) oriented toward expansion, which is the unfolding of mantra. Here, the sequence beginning with *vyāpinī* immediately after *samanā* is [the one intended by] the author of the hymn.
It is composed in a non-sequential order for the sake of conforming to the metrical structure, as it has been said:
"Śiva is indeed beginningless, the eternal abode, the first and immovable;
yet, O Goddess, when he expands by his own will, he does so without delay."
That power is supreme and subtle, the Transmental (unmanā), whose form is Śiva;
when it agitates its own self, which is mere existence, it brings about agitation.
She is designated as the *samanā* power, existing throughout all the paths;
she who, having withdrawn the universe, emits it once again.
The great power known as Kuṇḍalī.

Thus, the wise praise and establish you as having the form of the three powers; this is the implied meaning. Thus, in the first quarter, the traditional meaning according to the Trika system is as follows: He is desired and longed for by yogis as their own self due to His desirability;
thus He is Kāma, the Lord of Desire, Paramaśiva. He exists in her through non-difference from Himself.

Or, as the beloved (*kāminī*), she is non-different from her husband; thus she is Kāmeśvarī, the Primordial Beauty (*Ādyasundarī*). Alternatively, *kāma* refers to the desire for the sport (*krīḍā*) of creating the world, beginning with Sadāśiva and ending with the earth; she possesses that [desire], meaning she is characterized by the nature of creating the world and so forth. As it is said in the Rudrāyāmala:
"By her this universe is created," and so forth;

or else, she is called "Kāminī" because she desires—that is, she is oriented toward the desire to emit the universe, according to the Vedic scripture: "He desired, 'May I procreate many offspring from her. Furthermore, she is "Kāminī" because she desires, derived from the verbal root *kam*.
Because it has "beauty" (*kānti*) as its purpose, *kānti* means desire (*icchā*) and inclination (*ruci*); thus, [the Goddess] is one who possesses eagerness directed toward Kāmeśvara.
Alternatively, the meaning is that she shines forth in the form of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge, or as the nature of the wheels (*cakra*) beginning with Vāmeśvarī.
Or else, *Kāminī* is Bhairavī, the deity of the Northern Lion-Throne; her meditation is as follows:
"She is Kāminī, this Bhairavī, or the destroyer of fear"—
beginning thus, I shall describe her meditation to you.
She has a luster like that of the copper-colored sun, is adorned with jewel ornaments,
holds a noose, a goad, and displays the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons, and is seated upon the auspicious throne.
"One should contemplate the supreme Bhairavī, beautiful with a garland of severed heads.
Furthermore, Kāminī is the Yoginī in the form of Kāmeśvarī. As it is said in the Vidyārṇava:
"Now I shall describe Kāmeśvarī, who bestows the fruit of all desires."
And so forth: [He meditated upon] Kāmeśvarī, seated upon the moon, with eyes like darting wagtails,
eternally possessing a playful gait, beloved, and having the arrows of the flower-bowed god as her shafts.
...up to this point (p. 36).

Likewise, she is *kamalā* because the lotuses (*kamala*) are in her; [the suffix] *yac* is applied according to the rule for words beginning with *arśas*. She is thus Lakṣmī, who bears two lotuses, and has that as her form.
Alternatively, she is *kamalā* because she is desired by all; the suffix *kalac* is applied according to the rule for words beginning with *vṛṣa*. *Kaṃ*...

She is called *kamalā* because she bears (*malate*) the sun (*bhāskara*) with her splendor and nourishes him; or alternatively, because she is held (*dhriyate*) by the wind (*kaṃ*) through her speed. Thus, she is the embodiment of the power of illumination and velocity for those two. This is in accordance with the Vedic revelation: "By which fiery energy the sun shines," and "From fear of Him the wind blows" (with the variant reading: "From fear of Him the wind blows").

That which sustains Brahmā is called *brāhmī*, and its essential nature is *śakti*. The word *kaḥ* refers to Brahmā, the Wind (Vāyu), the Self (Ātman), Yama, Dakṣa, the Sun, a peacock, fire, and the masculine gender; whereas *kam* refers to happiness, the head, and water.
Thus, according to the *Medinīkoṣa*. Furthermore, she is called *Kamalā* because she beautifies (*malati*) Dakṣa Prajāpati with her birth;
that meditation is described in the twenty-second *śvāsa* of the *Śrīvidyārṇava*:
"She has the luster of rubies, [is flanked] by four lordly elephants resembling Mount Kailāsa, with jeweled [tusks] emerging from their trunks..."

May Lakṣmī protect [us]— she who dwells in a lotus, whose hands hold a pair of excellent lotuses and the gestures of protection and fearlessness, and whose lotus-feet are served by hosts of immortals.

Thus: likewise, she is *Kalāvatī*, because she possesses as her surrounding enclosure (*āvaraṇa*) the *kalās*— beginning with Kāmeśvarī and ending with Vicitrā— who are the presiding deities of the fifteen lunar days (*tithi*) starting from the first day (*pratipad*), who reside at the sides of the central triangle, and who are the powers (*śaktis*) denoted by the letters beginning with 'A'.

The meaning is that it is the sixteenth digit (*kalā*). As it is said in the *Subhagodaya*: "The fifteen digits beginning with the new moon (*darśa*) and ending with the full moon (*pūrṇimā*) are indeed [the first] fifteen; however, the sixteenth digit should be known as having the nature of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*)."
Thus, in the Tantrarāja:
"The other fifteen [vidyās] belong to the limbs of the primordial Lalitā;
by virtue of being her limbs, they possess a form that is common to all."

According to the statement in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (1.5.15, p. 37), "The Self alone is its sixteenth digit," and according to the Śiva Sūtra (1.3), "The group of matrices is the body of digits," [the individual soul] is characterized by its orientation toward karma.

Since the word *kalā* has already been explained, [the goddess] is "possessing that" (*tadvatīm*). Alternatively, she is the one who binds bound souls (*paśu*) by means of the *kārmamala* through the manifestation of her contracted power of action (*kriyā-śakti*). Or else, she is "possessing *kalās*" (*kalāvatī*), meaning she possesses all the powers of the universe (*viśva-śaktayaḥ*).
Thus it is said in the venerable *Maṅgalā*:
"His powers constitute this entire manifested universe, and the Great Lord is the possessor of power.
(17). And in the *Śrīśivasūtras*:
"The universe is the accumulation of His own powers. (3.30).

The *kalās* are the constituent parts such as the head, hands, and so forth; the Supreme *Kalā* (*parākalā*) is that which possesses them. Meditation upon her is as follows: "I bow to you, O Supreme Śivā, the Supreme *Kalā*, whose face is fashioned from the foremost point (*bindu*), whose pair of breasts is formed from other points, and who has the quality of the cord of the *nādabindu* as her seat."

Thus is the secret knowledge (*rahasyavidyā*). She is *Kalāvatī* because she possesses the *kalā*—either the digit of the moon (*candrakalā*)—which serves to revive her devotees; or else, *kalā* refers to the sixty-four arts (*kalā*) beginning with Akṣobhya, which are portions of the powers (*śakti*) such as Brāhmī and others, or she is endowed with those [arts]. Alternatively, *kalā* refers to the thirty-eight digits: ten of fire (*vahni*), sixteen of the moon (*candra*), and twelve of the sun (*sūrya*).

She is established in the ritual manual of worship (*pūjāpaddhati*), possessing those [qualities] and being of their very nature. Furthermore, there are other aspects (*kalā*) such as origination (*utpatti*), waking (*jāgara*), and so forth;
for example:
"Origination, waking, awakening, and the constant withdrawal of the mind."
The four digits are established in the waking state.
She is declared to be awake through all her qualities, yet she exists solely in the form of power (śakti).
Thus it is said:
"Death, forgetfulness, fainting, and sleep are enveloped by darkness (tamas)."
The digits of deep sleep are to be known; those digits are essentially Śiva.
Likewise, O Goddess, longing, delusion, thought, and recollection regarding sense objects— this fourfold set of arts is called the state of dream.

Those digits (kalās), which are of the nature of Śiva and the nature of Śakti, are essentially Tripura. Likewise: dispassion, the desire for liberation, meditative absorption, the pure mind, the discernment between the real and the unreal, and the fourth state (turyāvasthā)—these are the digits.

Likewise, in the section on the *Dūtīyāga*, the sixteen digits (*kalā*) are described as the internal messengers (*dūtī*) and so forth. Similarly, in the *Svacchanda-saṃgraha* and other texts, the [energies] beginning with the *bindu*, the half-moon (*ardhacandra*), and the *rodhinī* are said to be endowed with all those digits.
The meaning is "having that as its essential nature" (*tatsvarūpa*). Alternatively, the *kalās* [are distributed] among the five functions:
ten in emission (*sṛṣṭi*), twenty-two in maintenance (*sthiti*), eleven in withdrawal (*saṃhṛti*), and thirteen in the fourth state (*turya*).
Thus, their number is fifty; in the Light (*bhāsā*) which transcends them and is beyond all, [they do not exist].

Due to the absence of division, it possesses partlessness (*niṣkalatva*). Because this subject matter is extremely secret, the only refuge for its comprehension is the worship of the Guru; however, for fear of violating the secrecy, it is not disclosed here. As it has been said:
"In emission there are ten *kalās*, and in maintenance there are twenty-two powers (*śaktis*)."
There are eleven in the dissolution [phase], and thirteen in the fourth joint.
In the state of pure manifestation, where the splendor of the single, partless radiance shines forth, no conceptual construction arises;
yet, if it should manifest by way of reflection, there appears the Supreme Goddess, exceeding sixteen-fold.

Thus. Alternatively, the meaning is that she is "Kalāvatī"—possessing the thirty-eight *kalās* (energetic digits), calculated by summing five for Īśāna, four for Tatpuruṣa, eight for Aghora, thirteen for Vāmadeva, and eight for Sadyojāta; or else, she is Kalāvatī because she possesses the *kalās* of the phonemes from *A* to *Kṣa*, being thus the form of the supreme Great Mantra (*anuttara-mahāmantra*). Now:

And that is the meaning of *mātṛkā* consisting of those parts (*kalā*). This is the supreme, most divine power (*parā pārameśvarī śakti*) of the Lord, who is the mass of sounds (*śabdarāśi*) whose nature is full light; because it lacks outward orientation and is internal, it possesses identity with the subject (*pramātṛ-aikātmya*).
Mālinī is so called because, while manifesting the absence of the counter-correlate— the manifestation of the universe—
she assumes the process of the unfolding of the movement of the "vowelless" (anacka) [the letter *m*], and thus, with the desire to manifest the universe once again,
she bears it like a mirror and manifests the universe through the states of Parā, Parāparā, and so forth.

The Supreme Power (Parāśakti). Furthermore, she is "garlanded" (mālyate), meaning she is worn or held by the Rudras—the groups presiding over the letters from *na* to *pha*—and is accepted as their very self; or else, she "measures" (malate) the nature of enjoyment and liberation, or she "bears" (dhatte) it. Moreover, she is Mālinī, the garland of the three cities, the Mistress of the sixth wheel.

She is called *tadrūpā* (of that form) according to the grammatical principle of denoting a part by the whole (*nāmaikadeśagrahaṇanyāya*). Alternatively, she is *mālinī* because a garland (*mālā*)—specifically a flower-garland (*puṣpamālā*)—has arisen for her as the cause for the fruits of subjugation, attraction, and so forth; thus she is "flower-bearing" (*puṣpiṇī*). Or, she is *mālinī* because she bestows (*rāti*) or takes (*lāti*) that which is denoted by the word *mā*, namely *saṃhāra* (dissolution); since *ra* and *la* are remembered as interchangeable, the meaning is that she is the one who contemplates (*vimraṣṭrī*) the dissolution (*saṃhāra*).
As the venerable Ācāryapāda has said:
"She is garlanded (mālitā) by the Rudras; she is the bearer (dhārikā) of both supernatural powers and liberation;
she is in bloom with fruits; she is worthy of worship; and she is the six-legged bee at the sound of withdrawal."
Śambhunātha has declared that because the letters *ra* and *la* are endowed with the powers of withdrawal, bestowing, and taking away,
they should be remembered as one.

Thus, even within this state consisting of both Śiva and Śakti, there is a predominance of the nature of Śakti; for this very reason, its capacity to accomplish all siddhis is complete. As it has been said:
"Now I shall further proclaim the supreme ritual of Mālinī."
Subjugation, inciting enmity, eradication, paralyzing, immobilizing, and killing.
"By meditation alone, one becomes the Goddess.

Alternatively, *Mālinī* is another technical designation from the scriptures for the power of emission (*visargaśakti*) when it is agitated. This occurs when the wombs (*yoni*) and seeds (*bīja*), which consist of the objects of agitation and the agitator, undergo the process of agitation.

When, within the relationship characterized by agent and object, there arises an immersion consisting of their mutual fusion, she is called Mālinī because she assumes the nature of the universe. As it has been said:
"Because of the immersion into the state of the agitated and the agitator, they call her Mālinī."
Beautiful with the arising of emission through the union of seed and womb.
For Mālinī is determined to be the supreme power (parāśakti), whose form is the universe;
thus it is said:
"In all expiations, one should mutter the unbroken garland."
Whether it be divided or undivided, according to the relative strength or weakness of the transgression.

"O Dear One, from beginning with a single recitation up to three hundred thousand [recitations], what accomplishment (*siddhi*) would it not bestow, or what deficiency would it not fulfill? And furthermore:
"Because she possesses a garland (*mālā*), she is *Mālinī*; [the suffix] *iṇ* is applied according to the rule for words beginning with *brīhi*."
The name *Mālinī* belongs to the deity presiding over the fifty-one *mātṛkās*, or she is of that very form.

Alternatively, she is of the form of the goddess’s friend named Mālinī. This is stated in the *Vāmana-purāṇa*, in the section concerning the marriage of Pārvatī, regarding the taking of the seven steps: [Text follows]
Then the foot of Hara was seized by Mālinī for the purpose of receiving it;
Hara said, "What do you ask? Here, I give it to you, so let go!"
Mālinī said to Śaṅkara: "O Śaṅkara, grant this good fortune belonging to my own lineage to my friend; through that, you shall attain liberation."
Then Mahādeva said, "O Mālinī! I have given [you this]; release me.
Thus, *mālinī* refers to a specific type of meter (*vṛttaviśeṣa*), or it takes the form of the Mandākinī river;
furthermore, *mālinī* may denote a variety of meter as well as the wife of a garland-maker.

"According to the *Viśvakośa*: 'In the city of Campā, in Gaurī, and in Mandākinī, there is Mālinī. Because of the statement that 'she [the meter] consists of seven [syllables],' a seven-year-old girl is also called Mālinī; thus, she is of that form.
The meditation on Mālinī is as follows:"
One should meditate upon the auspicious Goddess, wearing red garments, possessing five faces,
endowed with the kalās beginning with Nivṛtti, and having three eyes on each face.
The Goddess holds a noose and a goad, possesses a skull-cup sprinkled with nectar,
is joined with the triad beginning with Will (icchā), and bears a trident in her right hand.
One should meditate upon the auspicious Mālinī, seated in the midst of a red lotus.
Thus, *lalita* (gracefulness) is a particular kind of charm (*vilāsa*) born from the emotion of love (*rati*) and other sentiments, as well as from mental agitation;

it consists either of the graceful arrangement of the hands, feet, and limbs, accompanied by the movements of the eyebrows and eyes, or it is the manifestation of such states toward a beloved lord of love. She who possesses this is *lalitā*.
"Lalita" means that she possesses extreme beauty or incomparable beauty; for the lexicon states, "In the three genders, *lalita* means beautiful. As it has been said:
"The name 'Lalitā' is indeed appropriate for you, for your divine activities are ever-new."
The bow is made of sugarcane, the weapons are likewise flowers, and everything is beautiful.

Thus [it is said]: Lalitā Saubhāgyasundarī. [The suffix] *yac* is applied according to the rule for words beginning with *arśas*. She possesses *lalita*, which is a specific type of action arising from amorous gestures (*śṛṅgāra-hāva*); therefore, this form has the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*) as its primary essence. Alternatively, she is *Lalitā* because she shines transcending the worlds. Or, she is so called because she dwells above, having transcended the masses of her own rays.
Or rather, she shines intensely in the forehead, in the middle of the station of the *bindu*. As it is stated in the *Pādmapurāṇa*:
"Because she transcends the worlds and resides in the forehead (*lalāṭa*), she is called Lalitā.
Alternatively, she is the Bhairavī named Lalitā. Her meditation is as follows, according to the *Śrīvidyārṇava*:
In the seventh *śvāsa*, concerning the deity of the southern lion-throne:
"She has the brilliance of a thousand rising suns and is radiant with a crown of rubies."
Adorned with jeweled earrings, pearl necklaces, anklets, armlets, and other ornaments.
Beautiful with jeweled anklets, clad in red garments and anointed with unguents,
she holds a noose, a goad, a book, and a rosary.

For the sake of attaining all prosperity, one should meditate upon the Goddess who is intent on childhood play, who assumes the form of a maiden, and who is beautiful in every limb. (Page 155-1-2) Thus, she is "Unconquered" (*aparājitā*), for she is always victorious in battles with the Daityas and other such encounters. Aparājitā.
Or she has the form of Jayadurgā. Alternatively, she is Aparājitā, because Śiva, Brahmā, and Viṣṇu exist as her couch-feet;
she is also the very nature of the Aparājita-vidyā.
[The term] Aparājita refers to that which is unconquered among the three, within the interval between Īśa and Ajeṣṭha.
Girikarṇī, jayā, durgā, and śataparṇī are used for a woman.
Thus says the Medinī. However, in the Devīpurāṇa:
"Having conquered the exceedingly powerful Daitya king named Padma, she became renowned throughout the three worlds as Vijayā and Aparājitā."

Thus, she is Vijayā, whose victory is distinguished in such a way as to be difficult even for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Purandara, and others to achieve; or she is of the nature of the bliss of the fourfold consciousness (*caturvidha-saṃvid-ānanda*). Alternatively, she is the very form of Śiva known as Vijaya, according to the enumeration of Śiva-tīrthas in the *Devīpurāṇa*, which states: "And indeed, Vijaya is in Kāśmīra. Or else:

The meaning is that she is either a specific temple named Vijaya well-known in the *Viśvakarmaśāstra*, or she is the *muhūrta* (astrological moment) named Vijaya, taking on the form of such a time. As it is said in the *Muhūrtaśāstra*:
"On the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina, at the rising of the stars..."
That time should be known as victorious, bestowing success upon all undertakings and goals.
The eleventh muhūrta, which is celebrated as Vijaya,
is the time during which a journey should be undertaken by all who desire victory.
Thus: because her nature is victory (*jaya*), the goddess named Jayā resides on Varāhaśaila;

she is called "Jayā" in the sense that she "conquers" (*jayate*)—that is, she is victorious, triumphant, and has attained excellence. Alternatively, she is the very form of the lunar day (*tithi*) known as Jayā, or she is the form of Śivā’s companion.
Or she is the nature of the fire-drilling wood (*araṇi*) endowed with the power to produce fire.
She is *Jayā*, *Jayaṃtī*, the goddess *Pathyā*, and *Umā* among her companions;
and she is born as *Agnimanthā* in the *Jayantī* constellation and as *Vijayā* for Yudhiṣṭhira.

Thus says the *Medinī*. Furthermore, the three goddesses beginning with Aparājitā are recorded as the retinue deities (*parivāradevī*) of Lord Tumburu within the Leftward Current (*vāmasrotas*). As it is stated in the *Śrīnetratantra*:
"She has four arms and three eyes, and she holds a *ṭaṅka* and a *kandala*."
And she shines resplendent upon a hungry ghost, holding a staff and a rosary in her hands.
Jayā is the goddess Vijayā, red in color, four-armed, four-faced,
and three-eyed, holding a bow and arrows.
The goddess, bearing a sword and a shield, is seated upon an owl;
likewise,
she resembles a split sapphire and is adorned with four faces.
She has four arms and three eyes, and likewise holds a noose and a goad;
with a jewel-vessel and a mace in her hands, she is well-seated upon a divine throne.
Clad in golden garments and adorned with golden ornaments—she is known as Aparājitā. (11 Adhikaraṇa, Sūtras 12–18)

Or, *umā* is the *lakṣmī* of Maheśa; she is called *umā* because she measures (*māti*), that is, delimits, and through her sovereignty makes known the Supreme Śiva (*uṃ paramaśivam*). Thus, the Śiva-nature is here called the "face" (*mukha*). As stated in the *Vijñānabhairava*:
"Just as by light [one perceives] a lamp, and by the rays of the sun..."
"Just as the divisions of the directions and so forth are known, so too, O Dear One, is Śiva [known] through His power" (Vijñānabhairava 21).
Thus says the venerable teacher Utpaladeva:
"For this very reason, He makes Himself an object of knowledge, appearing as if established separately."
The object of knowledge is not [the cause], yet its sovereignty is not compromised by being directed toward that object.
Thus, she is called *Bomā* because of the metaphorical identification with the color of the flax flower (*atasīkusuma*);
and because of her turmeric-colored complexion, she is [the deity] appropriate for meditation and other rites of immobilization (*stambhana*).
Or because she possesses the nature of fame and splendor; for it is said in the *Saptaśatī*:
"The Goddess who resides in all beings in the form of fame," or "in the form of splendor."

"Umā is so called because she was addressed as 'u' by her mother Menā when she was intent on performing penance in her childhood, and she was forbidden [by the word] 'mā'; thus she is Umā. This is stated in the Kālikā Purāṇa: "In the case of the daughter of Himavat, [the term] refers to turmeric, fame, and beauty. Here, "u" is used as a form of address, and "mā" is a prohibition; she is Umā because she was addressed and forbidden by her mother Menā when she had set out for asceticism in her youth. Thus it is said in the Kālikā Purāṇa.
Since she was dismissed by Menā to go to the forest for asceticism, that virtuous lady then received the name Umā from him, saying "O Umā! and "O Soma! (Soma = Moon).
In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa as well:
"But Aparṇā, being without food, her mother addressed her;
while forbidding her with the word 'Umā,' she then became Umā."
Having been addressed thus by that mother, the goddess, who had practiced difficult austerities,
became renowned in the worlds by that very name as one worshipped by the gods.
In the Puṣkara-khaṇḍa of the Pādma-purāṇa:
Then, from the sky, a divine voice spoke throughout the three worlds:
"O Mā! That which was said by you regarding your daughter has indeed been understood."
Therefore, its name shall be "Umā" among the worlds;
or it may be [derived from] "U," meaning supreme (*uttamā*), and "Mā," meaning the activity of the mind (*cittavṛtti*). Thus it is said in the *Sūtasaṃhitā*:
"She is the supreme experience that destroys the bonds of worldly existence, and she is exceedingly beautiful even for Sadāśiva."
I bow to Umā, whose mental disposition is supreme and who possesses manifold worldly splendors.
Thus; or alternatively—*Umām* refers to the Brahma-vidyā named Umā, who is traditionally known as the bestower of knowledge:
"In that very space, he approached a woman, highly resplendent, Umā, the daughter of Himavat" (p.
He said to her, "What is this Yakṣa? [Another reading is *kimetadyakṣam*]. "It is Brahman," he replied, and so forth, according to the *Kenopaniṣad* (3.12). In the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"Such is the supreme knowledge of Śaṅkara, which destroys worldly existence."
Indeed, it arises from the very faith of living beings and from their own power alone.

In the Sūta-saṃhitā, however, it is said: "That Śivā, whose form is knowledge, who is to be known through the Vedas, and whose nature is truth, bliss, and infinite consciousness— of that Ambikā, the sole mother of all worlds, there shall be [attainment] only through devotion by the grace [of the Guru]."

Thus it is said. Alternatively, because she is composed of the syllables that constitute the *praṇava*—which denote Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Brahmā—she consists of their three forms; therefore, the meaning of the *praṇava* should be applied here. For this very reason, those who know the secret call this word the "Devī-Pranava. As it has been stated:
In the *Liṅga-purāṇa*: "The syllables A, U, and M reside within my *praṇava*;
[they are] uttered in sequence as U, M, and A."
"Know my *praṇava* to be the three-measured (*trimātra*), the supreme protracted (*pluta*) [vowel].
Or else, according to the *Śivasūtras*, in the sūtra "Umā Kumārī is the power of will" (1.13), that which is called *umā* is the will of yogis; she is of that nature. As it has been said:
They declare that Umā is the power of will belonging to that very yogin who is perpetually swallowing the state of supreme Bhairava that has been described.
Thus, or alternatively: "Umā, the goddess of Vināyaka. According to the *Padma Purāṇa*, she who presides over the seat of Vināyaka is called Umā in the Sindhuvana forest;

or Umā is considered to be a six-year-old girl, as stated by Dhaumya in the section on maidens: "The daughter of the Ṛṣis, in the form of a maiden. They praise you with such names as these. The word "iti" [is used] here.
Even though they are intent upon the words, they declare them to be intent upon the meaning. || 22 ||
45) Now, raising the objection, "How can both enjoyment and liberation be accomplished for those who desire them?
[the author], indicating the sixfold meditation as the cause therein, offers praise:

I bow to the Blessed Lady Tripura, who possesses the brilliance of the fierce sun upon the lotus-thicket of the ultimate reality of unrestrained desire; who has mastered the sixfold transformations (or, according to another reading, "who has discarded the sixfold modifications"); and who is the playful cave of the lion of awakening intent upon the destruction of the lordly elephant of delusion. (23)
Transgressing the bounds of restraint (*dāman*), they are unrestrained and limitless; they are desired, thus they are "desires" (*kāma*).
Because they are sought after as the supreme objects of attainment, the various worldly and transcendental enjoyments are "objects" (*artha*);
and because the supernatural powers (*siddhi*) such as *aṇimā* are to be intensely sought after, these very things are the "clusters of lotuses" (*saroja-ṣaṇḍa*), that is, multitudes of lotuses.

In this context, "causing the expansion of radiance" refers to the goddess like the light of the sun with its sharp rays; just as lotuses reach full bloom by the sun's brilliance, so too is every desired object attained through the grace of the Blessed Lady. Of what sort [is she]? She is one whose sixfold [attendants] have been worshipped and served by practitioners (*sādhaka*).
She is the one who possesses the six paths of worship, such as those of the Śaivas and Vaiṣṇavas, which serve as the means for attaining that [state].
As it is said in the Kulārṇava:
"By means of those arising from the Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, Daurga, Ārka, Gāṇapatya, and Aindra [traditions]..."
For one whose mind is purified by mantras, the knowledge of the family (kula-jñāna) is revealed.
The Jaina system originates from Indu.

Herein the intended meaning is this: for those practitioners who performed the sixfold worship in a previous birth, once they attain the worship of Śrī Sundarī in this birth, there arises through the knowledge of the Kula the Siddhi of the Yāmala, consisting of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
It should be understood that the presentation of the meaning of the first and second halves of the verse was made with this intention (*āśaya*).
Alternatively, [the Goddess] is she in whom the sixfold varieties of phonemes—*ḍa*, *ra*, *la*, *ka*, *śa*, *ha*, and so forth—have been worshipped;
she who has performed worship in the form of the presiding deities of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) located within the pericarp of the six supporting lotuses.
Alternatively, the meaning is that she is worshipped in six ways (*ṣoḍhā*) by the powers of Gaṇeśa, the planets, and so forth, in six modes (*ṣaḍbhiḥ prakāraiḥ*), and thus she possesses their forms.

And yet, she who is the embodiment of the powers (śaktis) such as the expansion described in the *Mahāṣoḍhā*, or rather, who is worshipped in the form of the sixfold group beginning with the Supreme Lord and the Supreme Goddess according to the method of the lineage of the Six Śāmbhavas— the word "moha" (delusion) being placed first due to the rule of *rājadanta* (the last member of a compound being placed first)— is Māyā in the form of non-discrimination; that very [Māyā] is deep sleep, which, through its powerful intoxication, is like a lordly elephant (*dvipendra*).

There, the Lion— the awakened consciousness whose nature is the light of Bhairava’s own Cit, which has undertaken the exertion of its own heart and is intent upon slaughter and destruction— is the cave of play, the place of His sport,
through the abandonment of the state of contracted selfhood and the resting in the reality of full I-consciousness, which is the supreme light.
The meaning is "she who causes manifestation. Such is the Blessed Lady Tripurā—
Mahātripurasundarī— who is designated by the term "Tripurā" because she existed prior to the three powers, the three causal principles presided over by them, and the triad of states (avasthā).

Or, I bow to her named Tripurā, who consists of the nature of perfect *ahaṃtā* (I-consciousness), who is composed of indivisible self-awareness (*svasaṃvit*), and who presides over the *Trailokyamohana-cakra*. As it has been previously determined in detail, "The goddess Tripurā is one's own self-awareness. However, the meaning of "bowing" (*nati*) should be understood as consisting in worship through non-duality (*abheda-upāsanā*).
Anticipating the doubt, "Who indeed is this one named Tripurā who is to be resorted to with humble devotion?",
he points out that Supreme Deity, who is surrounded by her primary retinue of powers and resides within the inner sanctum:
"Praised by Gaṇeśa and Vaṭuka, accompanied by Rati, Sahāya, and Kāma, she is seated upon the excellent throne of the Enemy of Smara."

May Tripurasundarī, who is joined with the arrows of the flower-bowed god, surrounded by Anaṅgakusumā and the other goddesses, and accompanied by the three Siddhas, dwelling in the midst of the Kadamba forest, protect us. 24.

Gaṇeśa, the Great Lord of the Gaṇas, arose by the mere significant glance from the mouth of the Goddess at Kāmeśvara, in order to shatter the obstacles that had been imposed upon the gods by the demons. And it is said in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
Then the goddess Lalitā, casting a sidelong glance toward the face of Kāmeśvara, smiled, revealing her rows of teeth with great clarity.
Upon her face, which possessed the luster of a gentle smile, there manifested a certain god in the form of an elephant, with ichor trickling from the hollows of his temples.
p.

47) Thus it is said. Furthermore, Gaṇeśa and Vaṭuka, together with their Śaktis, are the Lords of the Field (kṣetreśa) stationed at the two door-posts of the Śrīcakra. As it is stated in the Saṃketapaddhati:
Victorious is the one Gaṇeśa, accompanied by his consort, who, like the sun, is capable of dispelling the night of the great delusion of duality and non-duality.
Victorious is that Vaṭuka, accompanied by his messenger and endowed with the *tāṇḍava* dance, who is the supreme radiance of inspired eloquence (*pratibhā*), like another moon.

In this context, by the expression "accompanied by Rati," it is implied that Gaṇeśa and Vaṭuka are also accompanied by their Śaktis. Thus, she is praised and extolled by them—Vaṭuka being well-known as the son of the Goddess and Kuleśa—and by the Gaṇas, the deities of the Gaṇas, such as Āditya and others mentioned in the *Ṣoḍhānyāsa*. As it is said in the *Agnipurāṇa*:
The Ādityas, Viśvedevas, Vasus, Tuṣitas, Ābhāsvaras, Anilas,
Mahārājikas, Sādhyas, and Rudras are the deities of the [divine] hosts.
Thus:
"served by the entire host of deities arisen from the Great Sixteen.
Skanda is the lord and leader of the *gaṇas*, that is, the *pramathas* such as Nandin, Bhṛṅgin, Ṛṭi, and others.

Is it Viṣṇu in the form of a young ascetic (vaṭu) or dwarf (vāmana), or perhaps the young ascetics such as the Bālakhilyas; or is it Brahmā, Vāyu, Dakṣa, Bhāskara, and Agni, worshipped by each with their respective sciences;
or is it the Gaṇas such as Nandin, Bhṛṅgin, and Ṛti, and the Lord Śiva, as well as Rati, the wife of Kāma?

"Accompanied by him" means accompanied by his minister, his companion—namely, Spring (Vasanta) or Kāma (Smara); "endowed with" means attended and honored by them through their respective arts. Here, by means of Rati and Kāma, the fifty powers of the Mātṛkās are indicated. Likewise, "the enemy of Smara" refers to the adversary of Kāma.

Sadāśiva alone is the excellent and supreme one; she whose couch (viṣṭara), bed (paryaṅka), and throne (mañcāsana) is supported by the four-legged [divinities] beginning with Brahmā—meaning she is seated upon the lion-throne consisting of the great corpse (mahāpreta) that is Sadāśiva. By the mention of his being a "couch" (viṣṭara), however—

The teachers state that, by way of intimating the state of being the support for Ānanda’s (Bliss) repose, a specific form of amorous constraint (*kāma-aṅka-yantraṇa*) is suggested; this is the secret reason why she is called Tripurasundarī. This is based on the Śruti: "This Self is Brahman; this very Self has four quarters. As it is said in the Bhairavayāmala:
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva—
these five great pretas are stationed at the soles of the feet.
Upon that most delightful surface of the great couch whose essence is Śiva, with Maheśāna as its pillow,
Sadāśiva himself was the mattress.
The four-legged servants, Maheśa, and the spittoon are there;
it is there that the Supreme Sovereign, Mahātripurasundarī, resides.

Thus it is said. The venerable Teacher (Ācāryapāda) has also stated this in such passages as "They have attained the state of the couch" (*gatās te mañcatvam*). Nor can it be here that these beings, beginning with Brahmā and ending with Māyā, [are meant], because it is impossible for them to rest upon the state of Śakti. Therefore, this is another form of theirs, not belonging to Māyā, which is appropriate for their status as the pedestal and feet of the Goddess.
However, it should be inferred that the form of both Īśvara and Sadāśiva is eternally transcendent of *māyā*.
As the venerable teacher Abhinavaguptapāda has said: "That form of Brahmā and the others previously mentioned is indeed transcendent of *māyā*."
This indeed should be the seat, and not one adorned with illusory ointments.
Above Rudra, one should install Īśvara as the deity, and above him, Sadāśiva;
he is called "the great preta" in the scriptures.

Because he pervades all the *tattvas*, he is the "Great Preta" (*mahāpreta*); because of his awakening and because he has reached the highest state, he is "merged" (*līna*), in that he does not descend to a lower level. (Tantrāloka 15.308–10) The word "he would go" (*vrajet*) means that he takes refuge in the supreme Śiva. This is the seat (*āsana*).

This is common to both the Left-hand (vāma) and Right-hand (dakṣiṇa) tantric paths. Likewise, she is endowed with the five flower-arrows—namely, flowers as arrows consisting of delusion, subjugation, and so forth; this is an elliptical expression meaning that she is beautified by four arms holding weapons. As for the nature of these weapons, it is of the character of mental impressions (vāsanā), as follows:
In the *Pūrvacatuḥśatī* scripture it is said: "His noose and goad are traditionally held to consist of passion (*rāga*) and hatred (*dveṣa*). Also in the *Tantrarāja*:
"The mind is the sugarcane bow; the noose is declared to be passion."
Hatred is its shaft; the five subtle elements are its flower-arrows.
Thus [it is said]. But in the *Uttaracatuḥśatī*:

"Holding the noose consisting of the power of will (*icchā-śakti*) and the goad in the form of knowledge (*jñāna*), and bearing the radiant bow and arrow consisting of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*)."
Thus [it is said]. But in the Vāmakeśvara [Tantra]:
"Sound, touch, and the other [objects of the senses] are his arrows; the mind became his bow."

Thus, in the Kādimata— [according to the reading "the arrows are of three kinds" (bāṇāḥ syustrividhāḥ) as edited by Ārthara Avalāna]— the arrows are said to be of three types, categorized by being gross, subtle, and supreme.
The gross [forms] consist of flowers, while the subtle ones are said to be of the nature of mantra.
Furthermore, O beloved, the gross [vāsanās] have been described within the vāsanā; listen to them:
the lotus, the white water-lily, the red water-lily, the blue lotus, and the mango—O Goddess, these are called the five flowers. (Pañcārthabhāṣya 5.48–50)
Their names are as follows:
Harṣaṇa, Rocana, Mohana, Śoṣaṇa, and Māraṇa; these arrows cause delusion even to sages.

Thus, in the Jñānārṇava it is said: "O Goddess, O Supreme Sovereign! [The powers] known as Kṣobhaṇa (agitation), Drāvaṇa (melting), Ākarṣaṇa (attraction), Vaśa (subjugation), and Unmāda (madness) are their names in due order."
Thus [it is said]. But in the *Tantrarāja*:
"Intoxicating, exhilarating, then deluding and inflaming, and withering—these are declared to be the five arrows previously mentioned" (Chapter 7, verse 13).
Thus, by means of Anaṅgakusumā and the others— namely, Anaṅgakusumā, Anaṅgamekhalā, Anaṅgamadanā,
Anaṅgamadanāturā, Anaṅgarekhā, Anaṅgaveginī, Anaṅgāṅkuśā, and Anaṅgamālinī— in the wheel that causes the agitation of all.
She is surrounded by the most secret powers (*guptatara-śakti*) who preside over the eight petals (*vasu-dala*), encircling her due to their close proximity.

She is also encompassed by the three *siddhas*, beginning with Mitreśa, and by the four lineage-gurus (*yuga-guru*), who are to be worshipped within the inner triangle known as the "Abode that Bestows All Siddhis" (*sarvasiddhiprada-dhāman*), because they are even more closely situated. She dwells in the midst of a *kadamba* forest, within the heart of the City of Śrī (*śrīpura*).
In a Kadamba forest adorned with Nīpa and other trees, like the Nandana grove, she sat upon an auspicious throne within a celestial pavilion situated in its center.

Śrī Tripurasundarī is the sovereign of the proclaimed cakras; she is called "Sundarī" because she shines forth through the state of aesthetic rapture (*sāmarasya*) as the universal self of the entire universe manifested within the three cities of waking and the other states.
She is the mass of consciousness and bliss (*cidānandaghana*), known as Lalitā, or alternatively, she is designated as the first "Sundarī" among the vidyās of the upper lion-thrones.
Tripura is Paramaśiva, whose three cities are the bodies of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva; his Sundarī is his beloved consort. As it is stated in the Kālikā Purāṇa:
"By the power of the Supreme Lord’s will, his body became threefold."
There, the upper portion became five-faced and four-armed.
In Maheśvara, the body of Brahmā has limbs as white as the filaments of a lotus;
its middle portion is blue-bodied, with one face and four arms.
In its lower portion, there appeared a Vaiṣṇava body with five faces and four arms, holding in its hands the conch, discus, mace, and lotus.
That body of the moon-crested Lord is white, composed of crystal and clouds;
thus, through the union with these three cities, the Supreme Śiva is called Tripura.

Thus [it is said]. Or rather, within the three cities—the domains of the knower (*mātṛ*), the means of knowledge (*māna*), and the object of knowledge (*meyapada*)—Sundarī is her nature eternally manifest because she is self-luminous. As it was stated by Abhinavaguptapāda:
"Therefore, consciousness itself consists of the triad [of powers], assuming the states of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge."
Grasping [the object], it shines forth precisely because its very nature is self-luminosity.
And that [consciousness], beautiful with the reflective awareness of the sound of the mantra which resides within it as its very self,
is indeed a valid means of knowledge by itself alone, because it is independent due to the absence of anything else.
Thus: "May He protect us"—the *loṭ* (imperative) suffix is used here in the sense of a benediction (*āśaṃsā*). || 24 ||

Thus, by means of the poetic figure *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic reason), he establishes that the worship of the aforementioned deity is fruitful for those desiring the fruit of the expansion of speech, following the description of her station and other attributes:
"Beholding you, who illuminate the expanse of the sky like a digit of the moon, appearing above the region of the forehead..."
O Bhavānī! You instantly make even those of dull intellect into wise poets; you are the wish-fulfilling cow for the lineage of those whose minds are fixed on meditation.
p.
51) O Bhavānī! This is an address to her who is the consort of Bhava, the Supreme Brahman, and his eternally inherent power (*śakti*).
In the reading *Mṛḍānī*, the meaning is "the one who grants happiness," as explained previously. [I bow to] you, the *kalā*...

She too was like a delightful digit of the moon— belonging to the moon (Indu)— shining near the forehead (anubhāladeśa), whose nature is the sky of consciousness (citākāśa) made radiant by that power which possesses the manifestation of the entire universe in its various forms.

Illuminating the expanse of the sky with their own radiance, the wise and discerning ones— those poets who, through the mere ripening of their meditative cultivation, instantly become endowed with the creative intuition for composing elegant sayings and excellent literary works characterized by true aesthetic flavor, sweetness, and the ornaments of virtuous qualities— gaze upon it as they contemplate.
[They] come into being. This very point is strengthened:

because you [are endowed] with *bhāvanā*, that is, the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the repeated practice of meditation in the form described; or else, *bhāvanā* is threefold, consisting of the Sakala, Sakalaniṣkala, and Niṣkala forms. As it is said in the *Yoginīhṛdaya*:
Everything up to the Ājñā-cakra is declared to be "with parts" (sakala); beyond that is the "partless-with-parts" (sakalaniṣkala).
In the supreme state at the end of Unmanī, the partless (niṣkala) exists in three ways.
Here, because it is said to be the region of the Anubhāla, [the state] is infused for those whose intellects are established through the contemplation known as the "entirety ending at the Ājñā."

It means she is like a cow that milks out all desired objects; she is to be fulfilled [as a source of attainment]. Meditation is to be understood as before. And the wish-fulfilling cow named Surabhi, by whose grace the sage Vasiṣṭha performed for King Viśvāmitra, along with his army and retinue, hospitality befitting a king.
These should be understood here by way of examples from the Mahābhārata; for the word "hi" (for/indeed) is to be supplied [in the text]. 25.
Now, raising the objection that if those with impure minds are unfit for the practice of *upāsana*, how can the desired fruit be accomplished?
Anticipating this, he prays for their purification— preceded by the removal of stains and the refinement of impressions— in order to render them fit for that very practice.
O Tripura, radiant as molten gold! Purify my ancient mind and cut down the forest of my multitude of sins.
For me, who am bound by shackles in this prison, may the fetters snap instantly upon the mere remembrance of you. (26)

(52) O radiant one! O beautiful one! O Tripurā! Just as gold (*kanaka*) is that which has been heated, melted, and purified—this etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) has been stated in many ways previously and will be explained further ahead. As for the etymological derivation of the word *Tripurā*:
O Vārāhī, you were worshipped in the past by the thirty gods, beginning with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa;
therefore, the name "Tripurā" was then proclaimed for you by the deities.
Thus [it is said]. Alternatively, "Tripure" is a locative form; the destruction of the three cities—the bodies consisting of the gross, subtle, and causal levels—is "Tripura.
In that [Tripura], there is a certain fourth power of consciousness (*saṃvit-śakti*) shining like molten gold; this is the vocative address: "O [Tripure]!"

O Thou of the luster of refined gold! Purify—make holy—the mind, my *mānasa*; that is to say, render it fit for the service of Thee. Likewise, cut down the forest of the flood of sins (*aghaughavana*), which has long existed due to its antiquity, being ancient and enveloped by the expansion of manifold latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

"Reap" means to render [the seeds] incapable of producing future sprouts. Indeed, the pacification of sin arises through the recollection and chanting of the Blessed Lady’s names; as it is said in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"Water is sufficient for the quenching of fire, and the rising of the sun for the dispelling of darkness."
The chanting of the names of the Goddesses is for the pacification of the flood of sins in the Kali age.
Thus it is said in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa: "For all committed sins, whether done knowingly or unknowingly,
the remembrance of the feet of the Supreme Śakti is declared to be the supreme expiation."

Thus, in the prison-house which is the abode of bondage in the form of *saṃsāra*, there are fetters and chains characterized by the impurities of karma consisting of good and evil deeds; the bondage caused by them is the assumption of various increasingly contracted levels of the subject (*pramātṛ*), and by that, one is afflicted through the experience of those respective afflictions (*kleśa*).

"May [the bonds] of me, who am suffering, suddenly and quickly snap—that is, be severed—due to the recollection of you and the meditation upon you, which serve as the cause. This is expressed in the *loṭ* (imperative) mood to indicate a wish (*āśaṃsā*). In this context, even auspicious karma is a means of bondage, just like inauspicious karma; as it has been said by the learned:
O Lord, please sever even my heap of merit, just as you have severed my mass of sins;
whether the chain binding my feet be made of gold or iron, there is no difference between them.

Thus [it is said]. Here, the locative case is used in the sense of cause (*hetu*). It should be understood that by means of these three actions, the removal of the three impurities (*malatraya*) is prayed for.
The meaning is that you alone are the liberator even from prison, just as the Goddess brought about the liberation of Aniruddha in the city of Bāṇāsura. As it is said in the *Harivaṃśa*:
"O Śāṅkarī, you are indeed celebrated by these names and others."
Through your grace, may I be swiftly released from bondage without obstacle.
Look upon me, O large-eyed one! I go to your feet for refuge;
you ought to grant liberation from all bonds indeed.
Beginning thus:
"In this manner praised at that time, the goddess Durgā, whose prowess is difficult to overcome,
liberated the hero Aniruddha who was bound in the city of Bāṇa."

Thus ends [the section]. Likewise, the story of how the princess named Ekāvalī was bound by the demon Kālaketu and liberated by her friend Yaśovatī through the power of the mantra of the Goddess she worshipped is recorded in the sixth book of the Devībhāgavata Purāṇa. || 26 ||

Thus, with the intention of showing what kind of object of meditation is appropriate for those who have attained purity of mind yet still desire worldly objects, he describes the fruitful meditative absorption (dhyāna) of the passionate type (rājasa):
"O Rudrāṇī! Those who contemplate you—whose radiance is crimson and whose form is non-dual—as if you were an image made of coral..."
Approaching them, young women with long-lashed eyes and tender vine-like arms clinging to their necks enjoy them by force. || 27 ||

The term *rudrāṇi* is an address meaning "O Śivā," the power (*śakti*) belonging to Rudra, the auspicious one who causes the destruction (*drāvayituḥ*) of the birth and other afflictions (*rujāḥ*). This address should be understood as being consistent with its reddish color;
therefore, such a comparison is expressed. [It is] made of coral, having the nature of *lodhra* wood.

The meaning is that she is like an image fashioned by Him, a reflection as it were; you, O Lady, possess a reddish luster, being crimson-hued and radiant with solar brilliance because you are devoid of rising and setting—according to the Śruti: "For there is no loss of the seer's seeing" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.23).
As it has been said:
"He whose light has not set is [the source] of both lights and darknesses. (p. 54)
He who is the one who dwells within and who is within that which is within, as well as light and darkness.
Thus: "pure, peaceful, and devoid of dissolution and emergence.
Likewise, "of non-dual form" means that whose other form is not different from ignorance—that is, incomparable.
Or, "of non-dual form" means of undivided form; by this, worship through non-duality is indicated. Those who contemplate and remember [her thus].

Those young women with beautiful eyes— meaning those who have reached the prime of youth— having approached those devotees of yours, serve them by force, that is, by means of compulsion; "pakṣmaladṛśaḥ" refers to those whose eyes possess eyelashes (*pakṣman*), the suffix *lac* being used here in the sense of possession.

The meaning is "they embrace. Of what sort are they? They are those whose creeper-like arms—slender and tender—are entwined and clinging to the neck (*kaṇṭha*) of the practitioner. Here too, this is intended as a description for the meditation on Kāmeśvarī. || 27 ||
He elaborates on that very point by means of another turn of phrase:

"Whosoever manifests your form—red as a blooming pomegranate flower, the imperishable deity of Love—even if he is devoid of physical beauty, young women with broad hips gaze upon him as if he were no different from the God of Desire himself. (28)
Your form is like the blossomed, fully opened pomegranate flower— the flower of the pomegranate creeper— red in color, smooth and crimson, having the god of love as its presiding deity,
being the imperishable syllable that is the presiding deity of the *kāmabīja* (the seed-syllable of Kāma).

He who would manifest that form— which is partless (*niṣkala*) and consists of the essence of *kāmakalā*— by contemplating it with excellence in his heart as non-different from his own self; him, though devoid of form, lacking the quality known as form, and even though deformed,
he is no different from the God of Love (*manmatha*), for he has transcended all distinctions through desire and is like the God of Love due to his loveliness.

Young women in the prime of their youth, with broad hips and slopes of rounded buttocks, gaze upon [the Lord] and approach Him; the meaning is that they wander about due to the delusion of passion (*madanabhrama*). Meditation (*dhyāna*) is to be understood as before. || 28 ||

Now, having raised the doubt as to what kind of meditation characterized by specific attributes (*lakṣaṇopāsanā*) should be performed, and while introducing its method, he expresses his own longing for it with uninterrupted intensity:
My two eyes are bound by the longing to perceive only Your form; my ears are impassioned by listening to the multitude of Your virtues; remembrance of You dwells in my mind;
my pair of hands possesses the skill of worshipping Your feet; Your praise resides in my speech; and everywhere, I have a passion for Your worship.
O Goddess! Let it not cease for me! || 29 ||

O Goddess! May there arise within my two eyes a bond of affection— a knot of love— toward that singular, primary perception of the quality of beauty in your form, which consists of the wondrous experience of the surging waves of the nectar-essence of loveliness, to the exclusion of all other objects of knowledge.
May my two eyes become solely intent upon the object of your physical beauty;

and may my ears— their function being the hearing of the "villages" (grāmas), which are the specific musical notes such as ṣaḍja and others arising from the throat— be occupied with the hearing of the multitude of your virtues when your qualities, such as valor and the like, are being sung.
"Passionate attachment" means that my two ears should become devoted to hearing the multitude of your virtues.
As for the characteristics of the *ṣaḍja* and other notes, it is said: "Touching the nose, throat, chest, palate, tongue, and teeth..."
Because it is born from six [factors], it is therefore known as *ṣaḍja*.
In the same way, the wind, having arisen and struck the chest and throat, reaches the navel; because it is situated in the middle, that great sound is called *madhyama*.
The wind, having risen from the navel, moves through the chest, heart, throat, and head;
by reaching five locations, it is called "fivefold."
Thus says Nārada:
"The peacock cries out the *ṣaḍja* note; cows bellow the *ārṣabha*;
goats and sheep [bleat] the *gāndhāra*; and the *krauñca* bird calls out the *madhyama*."
In the season when flowers are common, the cuckoo cries out the fifth note;
the horse cries out the sixth note (dhaivata), and the elephant cries out the seventh note (niṣāda).

Thus; or else— upon hearing, that is, upon listening to, the collection of qualities such as the heroism [displayed] in the slaying of Bhaṇḍāsura and others, the deeds such as the battle with and slaying of Mahiṣāsura, and the fivefold cosmic functions (pañcakṛtya) such as the creation and preservation of the world.

(56) "Attachment is the state of being colored by passion and having no other mental focus. This is an illustrative indication; therefore, the respective functions of the other faculties of cognition should also be understood accordingly. Likewise...
The meaning is: "May the memory [of you] arise in your mind, awakened by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the experience of various forms and qualities seen and heard;
that is to say, even when the activity of the external senses has ceased, may my mind become solely intent upon remembering you. This applies to the activity of the intellect as well.

This is an illustration. Likewise, regarding the pair of hands—skill, dexterity, and manual proficiency in the worship of Your feet, characterized by the offering of services such as perfumes and flowers—and likewise regarding speech, the chanting of Your glories; [all these are for the sake of Your service].
The ellipsis to be supplied is: "May there be a perfect description of your aforementioned qualities.
This also serves as an indicator for other activities of the feet, such as circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇā*) and so forth. As it has been said:
"The destruction of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, and the slaying of the demon Mahiṣāsura..."
Likewise, those who shall proclaim the slaughter of Sumbha and Niśumbha.
And so forth. In any place whatsoever, at any time, or in any state, may I have no addiction—
that is, no intense attachment— to your worship in the form of seeing, hearing, remembering, praising, and so on, as previously described.

"May it be stilled; may it be pacified; may it not exist"—this is the meaning. Thus, in such an activity of worship (*arcā*), the intended goal is for the group of instruments (*karaṇavarga*) to attain purity by means of a complete pervasion with full bliss (*pūrṇānanda*), preceded by the removal of impurity (*mala*), through being entirely and uninterruptedly devoted to the contemplation of the nature of the Goddess. As it has been said:
The great pervasion of supreme bliss, the falling away of all impurities,
the state of being the one who goes toward Śiva, the taking up [of the means], and the praise of Śiva as that which is to be attained.
The purity of the sense organs consists in this: the tasting, seeing, touching, and hearing of the abundance of the fragrance of Śiva alone.
Thus, even beyond that, the supreme purpose is simply the manifestation of the state of the Supreme Deity. Here, this word *mā* is not the particle *māṅ*;
therefore, there is no occasion for the application of the *luṅ* or *liṅ* tenses. It is the *loṭ* suffix used in the sense of an aspiration (*āśaṃsā*). 29.
He states that by merely reciting or even hearing this hymn, one becomes a partaker of the fruits of the previously mentioned practice of knowledge:

Whoever recites this hymn to the Goddess every day—which brings about prosperity—or even listens to it, for him his desired goal bears fruit; he is honored by kings and becomes most beloved by women with intoxicating eyes. (30)

He who is devoted to the Great Tripurasundarī— who is called Īśānī because she is endowed with full sovereignty (*pūrṇaiśvarya*), and who is called Īśvarā because she is not feminine by birth (ending in *ajādyadanta*) and thus takes the suffix *ṭāp* rather than *ṅīṣ* due to connection with a masculine—
daily and continuously performs that which results in the highest good, consisting of enjoyment and liberation, by means of his habit, inclination, and conformity toward her.
If one recites, proclaims, or hears this hymn of praise— which brings about welfare in this life and the next—

the maturation of the fruit of that recitation extends as far as its repeated cultivation; and since the hearing [of it] also culminates in the immediate practice of recitation and its resulting fruit, this is indicated by the word "daily" (anuvāsara).

It is awakened. Otherwise, there would be the mention of reciting it only once. His desired and cherished [aim] bears fruit—that is, it is accomplished. For he is honored by kings—that is, praised by rulers.
Of those women with intoxicating eyes—those whose beautiful eyes are like intoxicated *khañjana* birds.

"May he become the most beloved lover of those beautiful-eyed women with eyes like dancing wagtails"—here, the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is used in the sense of possibility. In this verse, through three actions, the threefold fruit of the practice of the *tryakṣarī-vidyā* (the three-syllable mantra) is described. || 30 ||
Now, for the purpose of auspiciousness, even at the conclusion of the hymn, he brings the praise to a close by reflecting upon his own state of total prostration before the Supreme Deity:
"To her who is worshipped by Brahmā, Indra, Rudra, Hari, the Moon, the Thousand-rayed One (the Sun), Skanda, the elephant-faced one (Gaṇeśa), and the Consumer of Oblations (Agni)..."
O Vāgīśvarī! O Mistress of the three worlds! O Mother of the universe, who has established Your abode both within and without—salutations to You!
Thus ends the second hymn, the Carcāstava, within the *Pañcastavī* composed by the venerable Dharmācārya. || 2 ||
p. 58) The three vocative terms— “O Vāgīśvarī!”, “O Tribhuvaneśvarī!”, and “O Viśvamātā!”—
correspond respectively to the meanings of the presiding deities of the three *kūṭas*.
This should be understood as being due to the intention of making [the Goddess] inclined toward the bestowal of fruits corresponding to each [individual].

Among the eight Sarasvatīs, one is named Vāgīśvarī; and she is the Universal Source (*viśvayoni*), for the Śruti states: "Speech itself, in that form, gave birth to all the worlds. Thus it is said in the Vāmakeśvara:

"O Vāgīśvarī, the power of knowledge (jñānaśakti) in the *vāgbhava* [syllable] bestows liberation"—from this statement, the meaning is that she is the presiding deity of the *vāgbīja*. Likewise: "In the *kāmarāja*, she is the power of action (kriyāśakti), Kāmeśī, who takes the form of desire."
Thus, the meaning is that she is Kāmeśvarī, the presiding deity over the seed-syllable of desire (KĀM). Likewise:
"In the seed-syllable of Śakti, the Supreme Power (Parāśakti) is indeed Will (Icchā) in the form of Śiva" (with "in the form of poison" as an alternative reading).
"Thus the Goddess Tryakṣarī is indeed Mahātripurasundarī. (4-17-18) This means that she is the Supreme Power (Parāśakti) who presides over the seed-syllable of Śakti.
"Brahman alone is this nectar in front; Brahman behind, Brahman to the south, and Brahman to the north."

"Below and above, this entire universe is spread out as Brahman alone, the most excellent"—so says the Śruti (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.11). Obeisance to You, by whom this established state—the existence both within and without—is fashioned through the nature of the higher and lower Prakṛti; [obeisance] to You from us.
It is hoped that there may arise a state of profound humility, characterized by the body, speech, and mind being entirely inclined toward that [Reality].

Alternatively, "within" (antar) refers to its presence within all beings in the form of the individual soul (*jīva*), according to the Śruti: "Having entered this very self by means of this living soul. Likewise, it exists "without" (bahiḥ) in the form of fire, water, earth, and so forth; or else, it exists "within" in a subtle form and "without" in a gross form.
Regarding "by form," the scripture says:
"The Goddess is subtler than the subtle and greater than the great.
And the Śruti says: "Subtler than the subtle, greater than the great" (Kaṭhopaniṣad 2.20).

Moreover, whether by way of the relation of cause and effect between the internal and the external, or by way of designating their non-difference—as in the Vedic scripture: "All this, indeed, is Brahman; it originates from Him, dissolves into Him, and breathes in Him; therefore, one should meditate with a tranquil mind" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.1)—it is all Brahman.

"Just as, my dear, by means of a single lump of clay, everything made of clay would be known— the modification being a mere verbal handle, a name, while the reality is simply 'clay'" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.4).
Thus, according to this Śruti, through the relationship of cause and effect, both are in fact one and the same.
The object shines; there is no other object whatsoever apart from that, according to the Śruti:
"There is nothing else higher than this" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.9).
This is Brahman, this is the field, these are the worlds, these are the gods, these are...

And from such scriptural passages as, "All these beings are this Self" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.6), [it follows that they are yours]. To what kind of you? To those for whom Brahmā, Vidhi, Indra, Śakra, or even the knowers of Brahman (indrā brahmavidaḥ)—those who, through direct perception, realize "I am Brahman," which is their own self—act as witnesses to this [Self] in its immediate presence.
"Indras! 'He saw this, he saw this'—therefore his name is Indra," so says the Śruti. Furthermore, Indra is the Self.
He beheld this very person as the pervasive Brahman, thinking, "I have seen this"; therefore his name is Indra. Indeed, his name is Indra; though he is truly Indra, they call him Indra.
Thus it is stated in the Śruti (Aitareya Āraṇyaka 2.3.13). Rudra, Śiva, Viṣṇu (by the word Hari), the King of Serpents, Dharmarāja, and Vāyu are included; and so says the Viśva lexicon:
"Hari [is used] for wind, the sun, the moon, Indra, Yama, Upendra, and the rays."
And among lions, horses, monkeys, frogs, snakes, parrots, and other such beings.
The word *hari* is declared to denote both the color green and the color tawny;
thus, its being worshipped by Viṣṇu is as stated in the Padma Purāṇa:
"Viṣṇu always worships the Goddess, who is composed of sapphire."
"By that [means], he attained the state of Viṣṇu," and so forth.
Candra is Soma, and Sūrya has a thousand rays. Regarding Sūrya’s state of being worshipped by the Sun, it is as stated in the *Padma Purāṇa*:
"By constantly worshipping with devotion the gem-like form of the Goddess, Divākara attained the divine and most auspicious status of Sūrya."
Thus, Skanda, Kumāra, Dvipānana, Gaṇeśa,
and Hutāśana— Agni— these twelve, beginning with Brahmā and ending with Agni, are the worshippers of the Śrīvidyā.

To her who has been saluted and worshipped by each [deity] with their respective sciences for the sake of attaining their own individual offices and positions— by this it is implied that even the acquisition of sovereignty by Brahmā and the others depends solely upon you, so what need be said of others?
Thus ends the second hymn in the commentary on the *Pañcastavī*, composed by the illustrious Mahāmāheśvara Paṇḍita Harabhaṭṭa Śāstrin.
A certain creeper shines alone among the three cities, its leading mass of spreading branches inlaid with leaves of shimmering, diverse colors;
it is that fourth [state] praised as one whose limbs are bent by the heavy burden of manifold fruits, while the others are merely the first.
The commentary is complete through the grace of others.
